title: Check category search demand and margin before starting any SEO work
hypothesis: If we confirm the store's main category terms have real search volume and the margin can cover months of work before starting SEO, then we avoid wasted content and link spend because SEO only captures demand that already exists.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells a brand-new product type with no existing search demand to capture

signal.check: No one has checked category search volume, margin and AOV against the likely cost of months of SEO work.

expected_effect.size: unknown, depends on category volume and margin

risk.note: This is a decision check, not a change to the live site.

prerequisites: Access to a keyword tool for category search volume
The store's AOV and gross margin
steps: List the store's main category and product-type search terms.
Pull monthly search volume and commercial intent for each term.
Compare category AOV and margin against the likely months of content and link cost.
Decide go or no-go on SEO for this category and record the reason.

test.method: Track organic revenue for categories that passed this gate versus any that skipped it.

title: Never tie a launch, restock or promotion date to an unranked SEO page
hypothesis: If we stop promising a launch, restock or seasonal promotion date based on a page that is not yet ranking, then the team avoids wasted promotion budget because organic rankings usually take months and cannot be scheduled like a paid campaign.

signal.check: A marketing calendar or promotion plan sets a date around a page that has not yet ranked.

expected_effect.size: cases in the source material ranged from under 100 days to 12 to 13 months before real movement

risk.note: Planning discipline only; no site change.

prerequisites: A shared marketing calendar the SEO plan can be checked against
steps: Flag any campaign, launch or restock date that assumes a page will rank by then.
Replace the date-based promise with a leading-indicator check instead.
Report progress on impressions and position, not a guaranteed date.

test.method: Review the marketing calendar each month for any SEO-dependent date.
test.measure: count of campaign dates tied to unranked pages

title: Report organic revenue and non-branded clicks, not raw traffic or rankings
hypothesis: If every SEO report leads with organic revenue and non-branded clicks instead of raw traffic or rankings, then the team catches a program that is not paying back because traffic and rankings alone can rise while revenue stays flat.

signal.check: The current SEO report leads with sessions, rankings or blog output instead of organic revenue.

expected_effect.size: one case ran 2 agencies at about $5,000 a month each for 2 years with traffic looking fine while organic revenue never passed about $2,000 a month

prerequisites: GA4 organic purchase tracking by landing page
steps: Add organic revenue and organic purchases as the top line of the report template.
Add non-branded clicks and money-keyword positions below it.
Move raw sessions and ranking counts to a supporting section, not the headline.

test.method: Compare organic revenue trend against traffic trend each month; flag any month traffic rises while revenue does not.

title: Build and optimize collection and product pages before writing any blog post
hypothesis: If we finish the collection and product pages before starting blog content, then organic revenue grows faster because shoppers land on pages that can actually convert instead of informational posts with no path to purchase.

signal.check: The store has published blog posts but its collection and product pages are still thin or unoptimized.

expected_effect.size: one case added about 40 new collection pages over 3 to 4 months and organic revenue went from about $2,000 to over $10,000 a month, self-reported

risk.note: Reordering work, not removing anything already published.

prerequisites: Keyword map with money pages identified
steps: List every collection and product page that should exist but is missing or thin.
Pause new blog post production until the money page list is optimized.
Build or optimize each money page using the collection or product template.
Only start the first content cluster once the money pages are live.

test.method: Compare organic revenue before and after the money-page push.
test.read_point: 8 to 12 weeks after the money pages go live

title: Fix the technical floor, then money pages, then one content cluster, then links
hypothesis: If the team works technical floor, then money pages, then one content cluster, then links in that order, then effort is not wasted on content or links for pages that cannot be crawled or indexed.

signal.check: SEO work is happening on several fronts at once with no fixed order, or links and content started before the technical floor was checked.

expected_effect.size: unknown, varies by store's starting condition

prerequisites: A written SEO plan or backlog
steps: Run the technical floor checklist (crawl, index, broken links, mobile UX, hierarchy) first.
Build or fix the money pages next.
Build the first content cluster only after money pages are live.
Start outreach and link work last.

test.method: Track whether each phase was completed before the next started; compare organic revenue for stores that followed the order versus ones that did not.

title: Concentrate content and link work on one category or cluster per quarter
hypothesis: If we finish sitewide hygiene once and then put content and link effort behind one category or cluster at a time, then that category ranks faster because effort is not spread thin across every category at once.
does_not_apply_when: The store has only one product line with no separate categories to sequence

signal.check: SEO effort is currently split evenly across many categories with no single one prioritized this quarter.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one source describes a 1-category focus over about 90 days

risk.note: Other categories are deferred, not removed.

prerequisites: Sitewide technical floor already fixed
steps: Pick 1 category or cluster to focus on this quarter.
Build its full content cluster and internal link plan before moving to the next.
Log the categories that are deferred and when they will get attention.
Bridge to the next category with a comparison post once the first is done.

test.method: Track organic clicks and rank for the focused category versus the deferred ones.

title: Never build a page for a product or category the store does not actually sell
hypothesis: If every planned page maps to a real product or collection the store sells, then the site keeps its topical authority because Google does not recrawl and demote pages built on categories with no matching catalog.

signal.check: The content or keyword plan includes topics or clusters that cluster near covered ones but do not map to a product the store sells.

expected_effect.size: one case ranked briefly on a shoulder topic then lost rankings on its original topic when Google recrawled

risk.note: Planning filter, no live pages need removing unless the mistake was already made.

prerequisites: Keyword map or content plan to review
steps: Review every planned or published content page against the real catalog.
Remove or redirect any page that does not map to a product or collection the store sells.
Add a rule to the keyword map process to check catalog fit before approving a topic.

test.method: Track rankings on the core topic before and after removing shoulder-niche pages.

title: Run SEO work on a fixed monthly cycle tied to what is on sale or in season
hypothesis: If we validate keywords, update pages and publish on a fixed monthly cycle tied to the season's or sale's category, then organic pages are ready before demand peaks because the cycle runs ahead of the catalog calendar instead of reacting to it.

signal.check: SEO tasks happen only when someone remembers, with no fixed monthly day or link to the sales calendar.

prerequisites: An inventory or sales calendar for seasonal and promotional categories
steps: Pick a fixed day each month for the SEO cycle.
Validate keywords for the categories on sale or in season that month.
Update those pages first, then publish new content and pursue links.
Give each tracked keyword about 6 months before adding support content or swapping it.

test.method: Compare organic readiness (page freshness, ranking) at the start of a season before and after adopting the cycle.
test.read_point: start of the next seasonal peak

title: Benchmark only against SEO competitors that outrank you for terms you both sell
hypothesis: If we pick SEO competitors as stores that outrank us for our own terms and sell what we sell, then keyword gap and link prospecting work stays winnable because giants like Amazon or Nike contain no closeable gap.

signal.check: The competitor list used for gap analysis includes marketplaces or category giants that do not sell a comparable catalog.

prerequisites: A list of who ranks for the store's money terms
steps: Search the store's money terms and note who ranks on page 1.
Keep only similarly-sized stores that sell the same or adjacent products.
Drop giants and marketplaces from the SEO competitor list.
Use this shortlist for keyword gap and link prospecting work.

test.method: Check the closeable gap size (Missing and Weak keyword tabs) before and after filtering the competitor list.

title: Protect position 1 for your own brand and product names
hypothesis: If the store holds position 1 for its own brand and product names, then paid ad spend stops leaking to competitors because shoppers who see an ad and later Google the brand land on the store, not a rival's listing.

signal.check: Search Console shows the brand is not in position 1 for its own name or product names, or a competitor appears above the brand for a branded query.

expected_effect.size: unknown, report separately from competitive rank

prerequisites: Search Console brand query data
steps: Filter Search Console queries to brand and product names.
Confirm the store's own page holds position 1 for each.
If a reseller or competitor ranks above the brand, fix the homepage and brand page and add internal links to them.
Report branded position separately from non-branded rankings every month.

test.method: Recheck branded query position monthly.

title: List every eligible product on the marketplace that already owns the SERP or AI citations
hypothesis: If we list a product on the marketplace that already holds first-page or AI-citation slots for its category, then the store captures demand it cannot win with a standalone page because fighting a marketplace for that slot rarely works.
does_not_apply_when: No marketplace holds meaningful search or AI-citation share in this category

signal.check: The live SERP or an AI answer for a category term cites a marketplace listing ahead of any standalone store.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one source estimates about half of product searches start on Amazon, unsourced

prerequisites: Product eligible for the marketplace's catalog requirements
steps: Search the category term and note whether a marketplace listing outranks standalone stores.
Check whether the product is already listed on that marketplace.
List any eligible product that is missing.
Route deeper marketplace strategy to the marketplace-specific playbook.

test.method: Compare category revenue split before and after listing the missing products.

title: Never compare SEO tool scores across vendors as if they were the same metric
hypothesis: If we stop comparing Ahrefs, Semrush and other tool scores against each other, then keyword and link decisions get more reliable because each tool's difficulty, authority and traffic numbers use its own formula and do not line up.

signal.check: A report or decision compares a Domain Rating from one tool against an Authority Score or Domain Authority from another as if they were the same number.

expected_effect.size: one example showed the same site at Ahrefs traffic of about 4,000 to 5,000 versus Semrush 9,800, and DR 44 versus Authority Score 35

prerequisites: None beyond the tools already in use
steps: Pick 1 tool as the source of truth for each metric type (difficulty, authority, traffic).
Label every reported number with its tool's name.
Never average or compare 2 tools' authority or difficulty scores directly.
Treat a tool showing 0 volume as a prompt to check niche knowledge, not as proof the term has no demand.

test.method: Audit reports for cross-tool comparisons before publishing them.

title: For a hero-SKU or thin-catalog store, treat the product page as the money page
hypothesis: If a store with 1 or a few hero SKUs treats its product page and cluster as the money page instead of building an empty collection layer, then SEO effort lands on the page that can actually convert because collections need many products to justify their own template.
does_not_apply_when: The store has 50 or more products where collections carry most of the organic revenue

signal.check: The store has 1 or a small number of hero products but the SEO plan still tries to build a full collection layer around them.

risk.note: Reprioritizes existing templates, does not remove pages.

prerequisites: Catalog size and structure confirmed
steps: Confirm the catalog is hero-SKU or thin, not 50 or more products.
Make the product page and its supporting content cluster the primary SEO target.
Skip forcing a collection template with no real content to fill it.
Route comparison and trust content around the hero product instead.

test.method: Track organic clicks and conversion on the product page versus any thin collection page over the same period.

title: List every eligible product in Google's free Shopping listings
hypothesis: If we submit a product feed to Google's free Merchant Center listings alongside organic SEO, then the store gets a second, no-cost slot on the same search results page because free listings sit apart from paid Shopping and organic results.

signal.check: The store has no Merchant Center product feed connected, or the feed is missing eligible products.

risk.note: Feed can be disabled at any time; no ad spend involved.

prerequisites: A Google Merchant Center account
A platform that can generate a product feed
steps: Create or confirm a Google Merchant Center account.
Connect the store's product feed (native app on Shopify, or a feed export on another platform).
Confirm every eligible product appears with title, image, price and availability.
Check for feed errors weekly until the listing is stable.

test.method: Watch free listing clicks and impressions in Merchant Center after the feed goes live.
test.read_point: 4 weeks after the feed is approved

title: Build and refresh seasonal category pages ahead of the season, not after it starts
hypothesis: If the content calendar is tied to the inventory and seasonal calendar instead of a fixed publishing day alone, then seasonal pages are indexed and ranking before demand peaks because search engines need lead time to index and rank new or refreshed pages.

signal.check: Seasonal or promotional category pages are built or refreshed only after the season has already started.

prerequisites: An inventory calendar with seasonal and promotional SKUs marked
steps: List every seasonal or promotional category and its typical demand window.
Set the page build or refresh date at least 4 to 8 weeks ahead of that window.
Add the seasonal calendar as an input to the monthly SEO cycle (SEO-008).
Request indexing after each seasonal update.

test.method: Compare organic clicks for the seasonal page at the start of the season this year versus last year's late build.
test.read_point: at the start of the next seasonal window

title: Classify every target keyword by intent and match it to the right page type
hypothesis: If every keyword is classified as informational, commercial, transactional or navigational before it is assigned to a page, then pages convert better because a blog post ranking for a buy query rarely converts and a bare product page ranking for a learn query bounces.

signal.check: Keywords are assigned to pages without checking whether the query is a learn, compare, buy or brand-reach query.

prerequisites: Keyword list to classify
steps: For each keyword, decide if it is informational, commercial, transactional or navigational.
Route informational queries to blog or guide pages.
Route transactional and commercial queries to collection and product pages.
Flag any existing page whose type does not match its main keyword's intent for a fix.

test.method: Track bounce rate and conversion on pages before and after fixing an intent mismatch.

title: Read the live SERP before building any page and match its format
hypothesis: If we check the top 10 live results for a target keyword before building the page, then the new page has a real chance to rank because the page type follows what already ranks instead of guessing.

signal.check: A page is being planned or refreshed without a fresh incognito search of its target keyword.

prerequisites: An incognito browser set to the target country
steps: Search the exact target keyword in an incognito window set to the target country.
Classify the top 10 organic results by format (product, collection, guide, video, forum).
If 5 or more share one format, build that format; if mixed, pick the format the store's authority can win.
If only giants rank, skip the term or pick a more specific variant.
Note any AI Overview, video carousel or shopping results present.
Record the format, features and check date on the keyword map.

test.method: Recheck rankings 8 weeks after publishing a page built to match the SERP format.

title: Answer the visitor's search intent in the first screen of every page
hypothesis: If the first visible screen of a page names the product, price and the answer to the query, then fewer visitors click back to the search results because a shopper who bounces back is a signal against the page.

signal.check: The top of a money page opens with a tagline or generic hero image instead of the product name, price and a clear answer to the query.

risk.note: Above-the-fold copy and layout change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Access to edit the page's first-fold section
steps: Identify the query the page targets and what a shopper wants to see first.
Put the product or category name, price and 1 clear call to action above the fold.
Remove any tagline-only or vague hero copy that does not answer the query.
Re-check the page on mobile, where the fold is shortest.

test.method: Compare pogo-sticking (immediate back-clicks) and bounce rate before and after the change.

title: Build a roundup or comparison page to break into a term owned by enterprise homepages
hypothesis: If the SERP for a commercial term is mixed and includes listicles, then a tested, screenshot-backed roundup page can outrank enterprise homepages because a bigger brand's homepage is not automatically the best answer to a comparison query.
does_not_apply_when: The SERP is entirely dominated by giant homepages with no listicle or roundup format present

signal.check: The live SERP for a commercial term mixes enterprise homepages with listicle or roundup content.

expected_effect.size: one case outranked 2 larger competitors' homepages for a commercial term with a tested, screenshot-backed roundup

risk.note: Listing competitors sends some readers to them; write it factually and keep the brand's own offer first.

prerequisites: P5 SERP check confirms a mixed, listicle-friendly SERP
steps: Confirm the SERP includes listicle or roundup pages alongside enterprise homepages.
Write a tested, first-hand roundup with screenshots or real product photos.
List the store's own product first with claims it can support.
Publish and link the roundup from the relevant money page.

test.method: Track ranking and clicks for the roundup page against the term's SERP.

title: Log the store's own speed baseline instead of adopting a presenter's fixed target
hypothesis: If the store logs its own dated speed baseline and follows the dedicated speed playbook's protocol instead of copying a single number a presenter used, then speed decisions are based on this store's own data because sources gave targets ranging from 1 second to Lighthouse 100, with none proven universal.

signal.check: A speed target is being adopted from a course or video (for example, "under 3 seconds" or "Lighthouse 100") instead of the store's own baseline and the dedicated speed protocol.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources gave targets from 1 to 2 seconds up to Lighthouse 100, none proven as a universal number

prerequisites: A dated speed baseline (see the dedicated speed playbook)
steps: Log LCP, CLS, INP and TTFB for the store's key pages with a date.
Reject any single fixed target copied from a course or demo as a universal number.
Use the store's own baseline and trend as the target to beat.
Follow the dedicated speed playbook's protocol for deeper work.

test.method: Compare the store's own speed metrics against its own prior baseline, not an external target.

title: Run a full Google Business Profile program for any store with a physical location
hypothesis: If a store with a physical location claims and completes its Google Business Profile, posts weekly, asks for reviews in person and replies to every review, then local visibility and trust improve because an incomplete or unclaimed profile is a lowest-hanging-fruit opportunity left on the table.
does_not_apply_when: The store is a pure online retailer with no physical location

signal.check: The store has a physical location but its Google Business Profile is unclaimed, incomplete, rarely posted to, or reviews go unanswered.

prerequisites: Confirmed physical location
Access to claim the Google Business Profile
steps: Claim and fully complete the Google Business Profile (hours, categories, photos, description).
Post to the profile weekly.
Ask customers for reviews in person after a purchase or visit.
Reply to every review, positive or negative.
Keep NAP consistent with the citation set (SEO-105).

test.method: Track review count, rating and profile views over time after starting the program.

title: Score every candidate keyword on demand, fit, intent and difficulty
hypothesis: If every keyword is scored on demand, fit, intent and difficulty before it enters the plan, then time is not spent building pages for terms that fail 1 of these 4 checks.

signal.check: Keywords are added to the plan straight from a volume-sorted export with no scoring against fit, intent and difficulty.

prerequisites: A raw keyword export
steps: Score each keyword on demand (volume), fit (do we sell this), intent (does it match a page type we can build) and difficulty.
Keep only keywords that pass all 4 checks for the main plan.
Move single-attribute keywords to a top-of-funnel list with a conversion path attached.

test.method: Compare ranking success rate for scored keywords versus unscored ones added in the past.
test.read_point: 3 months after building pages for scored keywords

title: Mine free keyword sources before paying for a keyword tool
hypothesis: If we pull Search Console queries, autocomplete, People Also Ask and Keyword Planner data before buying a paid tool, then the keyword map starts from Google's own data because Search Console is the most accurate source available.

signal.check: Keyword research starts directly with a paid tool export, skipping the store's own Search Console query data.

prerequisites: Search Console access
A free Google Ads account for Keyword Planner
steps: Export the last 16 months of Search Console queries.
Record autocomplete, People Also Ask and "people also search for" for each seed term.
Run each seed through Keyword Planner with the target country set.
Note relevant phrasing found on Reddit or forums.
Only then run the paid tool for expansion and difficulty scores.

test.method: Compare the share of the final keyword map sourced from free tools versus paid.
test.read_point: after the keyword map is built

title: Set the keyword difficulty ceiling and volume floor from the store's catalog and margin
hypothesis: If the difficulty ceiling and volume floor are set from the store's own authority, catalog size and margin instead of copying a presenter's number, then the keyword list stays realistic because a niche 50-product store cannot demand 5,000 searches a month on every term.

signal.check: The keyword gate uses a fixed volume floor or difficulty ceiling copied from a course or tool demo, not calculated from this store's catalog and authority.

expected_effect.size: sources gave floors from 100 to 5,000 searches a month and difficulty ceilings from 30 to 49; none is a universal number

prerequisites: Store catalog size, margin and current domain authority
steps: Check the store's current keyword difficulty ranking ability (new or low-authority: keep difficulty under 30 to 40).
Set a volume floor the catalog can support; do not copy 500, 1,000 or 5,000 from a demo.
Require intent to match the page type being built.
Write the floor and ceiling at the top of the keyword map sheet.

test.method: Track how many keywords pass the gate and how many later rank, then adjust the floor and ceiling.
test.read_point: quarterly review of the keyword map

title: Look for gold-nugget keywords with near-zero difficulty and real volume, then sanity check them
hypothesis: If we scan the keyword export for terms with near-zero difficulty and real volume, then we find easy wins because tools sometimes underscore a term's difficulty when it actually contains a brand name or is harder than it looks.

signal.check: The keyword export has not been scanned specifically for low-difficulty, high-volume outliers.

expected_effect.size: one example found a term at 14,800 searches a month with near-zero difficulty

prerequisites: A keyword tool export with difficulty scores
steps: Sort the keyword export by difficulty ascending, then by volume descending.
Flag any term with near-zero difficulty and meaningful volume.
Check by hand whether the term contains a brand name or is otherwise harder than the score suggests.
Add confirmed gold-nugget terms to the priority list.

test.method: Track how fast gold-nugget terms rank compared to normally-gated terms.

title: Use CPC as a secondary commercial-intent signal, not the only keyword filter
hypothesis: If CPC is used only as a secondary commercial-intent signal alongside difficulty and intent, then money keyword selection stays accurate because a high CPC by itself can also be bad data.

signal.check: Keywords are filtered by a hard CPC cutoff with no other checks, or a very high CPC outlier is trusted without question.

expected_effect.size: one source flagged a $700 CPC as bad data against a typical $3 to $20 range in that niche

prerequisites: CPC data from a keyword tool
steps: Use CPC over a low threshold (about $1) as one signal of commercial intent, not a sole filter.
Flag CPC outliers far outside the category's typical range and check them by hand before trusting them.
Use Keyword Planner's low-end bid as a competition proxy when no difficulty score exists.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on pages targeting high-CPC terms confirmed as real commercial intent versus outlier terms.
test.read_point: after enough traffic accumulates on the target pages

title: Hand-sweep every keyword export to remove irrelevant and competitor-brand terms
hypothesis: If a person manually sweeps every keyword export to remove competitor brand names, mascots, job-seeker queries and out-of-catalog terms, then the keyword map stops wasting effort on terms the store cannot legitimately win or should not chase.

signal.check: The keyword list still contains competitor brand names, mascots, job-seeker phrases or products the store does not sell.

prerequisites: A raw keyword export
steps: Read every row of the export by hand after the tool filter runs.
Remove competitor brand names, mascots and job-seeker queries.
Remove any term for a product or region the store does not sell or ship to.
Repeat this sweep after every new export, not just once.

test.method: Recount irrelevant terms in the next export after adding this step to the process.

title: Give every page exactly 1 primary keyword plus a cluster of secondary terms
hypothesis: If each page targets 1 primary keyword and a cluster of secondaries in its copy, then pages stop competing with each other because keyword stuffing 1 term across many pages splits ranking signal instead of building it.

signal.check: Two or more pages target the same primary keyword, or 1 page tries to rank for several unrelated topics at once.

prerequisites: Keyword map with primary and secondary columns
steps: Assign exactly 1 primary keyword to each page (title, H1, URL).
Group 3 to 5 secondary terms around it for use in the body copy.
Split genuinely different topics onto separate pages instead of stuffing 1 page.
Check the map for any 2 rows sharing a primary keyword and merge or re-target one.

test.method: Check Search Console for pages with unstable ranking URLs on 1 query, a sign of cannibalization, before and after the fix.

title: Build a topical map with cluster, page type and status columns instead of a flat keyword list
hypothesis: If keywords are organized into a topical map with cluster, page type, URL, volume, rank and status columns, then the team always knows what to publish next because the map replaces guesswork with a status-tracked plan.

signal.check: The keyword list is a flat spreadsheet with no cluster, page type or status columns.

prerequisites: A scored and swept keyword list
steps: Group keywords into clusters that share a SERP or a meaning.
Add columns for page type, primary keyword, secondaries, URL, volume, current rank and status.
Set status values: published, needs refresh, quick win, needs publishing.
Assign an owner and priority tier to each row.

test.method: Track how many rows move from needs-publishing to published each month after adopting the map.

title: Run a keyword gap analysis against SEO competitors and pursue only gaps you can sell
hypothesis: If we run a keyword gap against real SEO competitors and only chase gaps for products we sell, then new content targets terms with a proven market because a competitor already ranks and converts on it.

signal.check: No keyword gap analysis has been run against the store's SEO competitors, or gap terms for products the store does not sell are still on the plan.

expected_effect.size: one example found 931 common keywords versus a competitor's 2,953, with 1 named term the client did not cover

prerequisites: A tool with a keyword gap feature
A vetted SEO competitor list (SEO-009)
steps: Run a keyword gap report against 3 to 4 named SEO competitors.
Review the Missing (they rank, you do not) and Weak (you rank far below) tabs.
Keep only gap terms for products the store actually sells.
Add the kept gaps to the topical map with priority tier.

test.method: Track how many gap terms move to ranking within 3 to 6 months.
test.read_point: 3 to 6 months after adding gap terms to the plan

title: Start from a shortlist of money terms, then expand each into its long-tail cluster
hypothesis: If the keyword roadmap starts from a short list of business-driving terms and expands each into a long-tail cluster, then priority stays on the terms that matter most because working a volume-sorted list top to bottom spreads authority thin across unrelated topics.

signal.check: The keyword roadmap is a volume-sorted list worked from the top down with no shortlist of priority money terms.

prerequisites: Full keyword list already gathered
steps: Pick a shortlist of business-driving terms by tier: brand, hero products, category heads.
Expand each shortlisted term into its own long-tail and question cluster.
Sequence work by shortlist tier, not by raw volume ranking.

test.method: Track organic revenue contribution from shortlist-driven clusters versus any volume-sorted leftovers.

title: Use AI to organize keyword exports, never to invent keyword data
hypothesis: If keyword volume and difficulty always come from a real tool export and AI is used only to organize that export into a plan, then the keyword map avoids invented numbers because a chat model cannot supply real search volume data on its own.

signal.check: Someone has asked an AI chat directly for keyword ideas or volumes without feeding it a real tool export.

prerequisites: A real keyword tool export as the AI's input
steps: Pull volume, difficulty and intent from a real keyword tool first.
Feed the raw export into an AI chat with the store's business context.
Ask for a money page, subpage and article structure from that data.
Answer any clarifying questions the model asks before accepting its output.

test.method: Audit any AI-suggested keyword for a matching real tool data point before it enters the plan.

title: Mine People Also Ask and Search Console questions for FAQ and content ideas
hypothesis: If we mine People Also Ask and a Search Console question-word regex for real questions, then FAQ sections and content ideas match what shoppers actually ask because they come from real queries instead of invented ones.

signal.check: FAQ sections are written from guesswork instead of real People Also Ask or Search Console question data.

expected_effect.size: one example found 558 questions from 1 seed term

prerequisites: Search Console access
A question-research tool or People Also Ask
steps: Pull People Also Ask questions for each target keyword.
Filter Search Console queries with a regex for who, what, when, where, why, how, can, does.
Pick 3 to 4 questions per cluster for the FAQ section or content plan.
Add an FAQ or new page anywhere the site surfaces a question with no answering page.

test.method: Track impressions and clicks on question-based queries after adding matching FAQ content.

title: Re-run keyword research after any catalog change and recheck tracked terms on a schedule
hypothesis: If keyword research is re-run whenever the catalog changes, then the keyword map stays accurate because volume, difficulty and rankings shift and a map built for last year's catalog can miss new products or drop discontinued ones.

signal.check: Products have been added or discontinued since the keyword map was last updated.

prerequisites: A catalog change log
steps: Add a keyword-map review step to every catalog change (new product line, discontinued SKUs).
Recheck tracked keywords' rank, volume and difficulty on a fixed schedule.
Give a keyword about 6 months before changing course or swapping it for a different target.

test.method: Check the keyword map's age and last-review date against the catalog's most recent change.
test.read_point: at every catalog change and every 6 months

title: Only target a top-of-funnel keyword when a conversion path exists behind it
hypothesis: If every high-volume informational keyword is paired with a real conversion path (a download, an email capture, a linked product), then top-of-funnel traffic stops being vanity because it now feeds a nurture or purchase flow.

signal.check: A high-volume informational keyword is targeted with no linked offer, email capture or product path.

expected_effect.size: one example paired a 300,000-search term with a template download, email capture and nurture flow

risk.note: Adds a path to existing content, no removal needed.

prerequisites: An email capture or product-linking mechanism on the page
steps: List every top-of-funnel keyword in the plan.
For each, name the specific conversion path (download, capture, linked product) it will use.
Drop or deprioritize any TOFU term with no path attached.
Add the path to the page brief before the page is built.

test.method: Track email captures or assisted conversions from TOFU pages with a path versus those without.

title: Audit existing pages for wasted rankings and re-aim or fix them
hypothesis: If we audit what existing pages already rank for in Search Console, then wasted content gets fixed because a page ranking for a zero-volume or irrelevant term can be re-aimed at a real money term instead of left alone.
does_not_apply_when: The store has no content history yet to audit

signal.check: No one has checked which queries existing pages actually rank for against their intended target keyword.

risk.note: Audit and retarget, previous copy can be restored from a saved version.

prerequisites: Search Console query data by page
Existing content inventory
steps: Pull the queries each existing page actually ranks for from Search Console.
Flag pages ranking for zero-volume or irrelevant terms.
For each flagged page, decide consolidate, upgrade or delete based on the data, not gut feel.
Re-aim the title, H1 and content toward the real click-earning query where one exists.

test.method: Compare clicks on re-aimed pages before and after the change.

title: Draw the full site architecture tree before building or restructuring the catalog
hypothesis: If the home, collection, subcollection and product tree is planned on paper before building, then months of rework are avoided because every page gets 1 parent and a planned link path from the start.

signal.check: The store is launching, replatforming or restructuring its catalog with no written page tree.

prerequisites: Keyword map with cluster and page-type assignments
steps: Draw home, collections, subcollections and products as a tree with 1 parent per page.
Derive the structure from the topical map, not from a copied competitor menu.
Note the planned link path from home to every product.
Review the tree with whoever owns theme or platform changes before building.

test.method: Check for orphan pages and duplicate-keyword pages in the first crawl after building against the plan.
test.read_point: first crawl after launch or restructure

title: Assign collection, product and homepage URLs by query breadth
hypothesis: If broad and option-seeking terms go to collections, specific terms go to products, and only 1 broad term with no collection match goes to the homepage, then each page targets the right breadth of query and stops competing with its siblings.

signal.check: A broad category term is assigned to a product page, or a specific product term is assigned to a collection.

expected_effect.size: one example sent a 14,000-search broad term to a collection and a 490-search specific term to a product

prerequisites: Keyword map with volume per term
steps: Sort keywords by search volume and specificity.
Assign the broadest, option-seeking terms to collection pages.
Assign specific product and attribute terms to product pages.
Reserve the homepage for at most 1 broad term no collection also targets.

test.method: Recheck rankings for pages whose URL type was corrected.

title: Fix keyword cannibalization by giving every topic exactly 1 page
hypothesis: If no 2 pages target the same keyword, then rankings stabilize because an unstable ranking URL for 1 query in Search Console is the clearest sign 2 pages are competing with each other for the same term.

signal.check: Search Console shows the ranking URL for 1 query switching between 2 or more pages.

risk.note: Merging or redirecting a page can lose its own small ranking; check both pages' individual value first.

prerequisites: Search Console query-by-page data
steps: Filter Search Console by the query showing unstable ranking URLs.
Identify the 2 or more competing pages.
Pick the stronger page as the single target and merge, redirect or re-target the other.
Do not fix cannibalization by repeating the keyword on more pages.

test.method: Recheck the query's ranking stability 4 to 8 weeks after consolidating.

title: Split a collection into subcollections only when each split has its own demand and content
hypothesis: If a collection is only split into subcollections that each have their own search demand and unique content, then the new pages have a real chance to rank instead of becoming thin 'on sale' or 'top rated' clones with no unique value.

signal.check: The store has or plans subcollection pages like "top rated" or "on sale" with no distinct search demand or unique copy.

risk.note: Existing thin pages can be merged back into the parent.

prerequisites: Keyword volume data per potential subcollection
steps: Check search volume for each candidate subcollection split.
Keep only splits with their own demand and enough products to fill unique content.
Write unique copy for each kept subcollection; link it from the parent.
Merge or noindex any modifier page with no unique value (a blog post can cover it instead).

test.method: Track rankings and clicks for the kept subcollections versus the retired modifier pages.

title: Give real collection pages to any filter combination with its own demand
hypothesis: If any filter combination with real search demand gets a true collection page instead of relying on a Shopify parameter URL, then that demand can be captured because parameter-based filter URLs are not indexed and cannot carry unique content.
does_not_apply_when: The collection has fewer than about 200 SKUs and no filter combination shows real demand

signal.check: A collection has 200 or more SKUs with popular filter combinations that only exist as parameter URLs.

risk.note: New collection pages, existing filter URLs keep working.

prerequisites: Faceted navigation app or feature (Shopify Search and Discovery)
steps: List filter combinations with meaningful search volume.
Build a real collection page for each combination worth ranking.
Link the new pages from the parent collection and the menu.
Leave low-demand filter combinations as unindexed parameter URLs.

test.method: Track indexed page count and clicks on the new facet-based collections.

title: Noindex Shopify's auto-generated tag, vendor and utility pages
hypothesis: If Shopify's auto-generated tag, vendor, product-type and utility pages carry noindex, follow, then crawl budget stops going to pages that can never carry a unique title, H1 or copy.

signal.check: Search Console's Pages report shows tag, vendor, product-type, all-collections, all-products or new-products pages indexed.

risk.note: Theme snippet edit, revert by removing the noindex line.

prerequisites: Theme code access
A duplicate theme to test on first
steps: Identify every Shopify auto-generated tag, vendor, type and utility page class.
Add noindex, follow snippets for these page classes in theme.liquid.
Build a real collection page for any tag topic that is actually worth ranking.
Recheck the Pages report a week later to confirm the classes move to excluded.

test.method: Compare indexed-page count for these classes before and after the fix.

title: Fix Shopify's duplicate product URLs and rebuild breadcrumbs from a metafield
hypothesis: If we remove within_collection from the product grid snippet and rebuild breadcrumbs from a stored metafield, then crawl waste drops because every collection path to a product stops being crawled as a separate duplicate URL.

signal.check: Opening the same product from 2 different collections shows 2 different URLs (/collections/x/products/y) instead of a clean /products/y path.

risk.note: Breaks URL-derived breadcrumbs; must add a metafield-based rebuild in the same change; test on a duplicate theme first.

prerequisites: Theme code access
Metaobject and metafield definitions on Products
steps: Open the same product from 2 collections and confirm the duplicate-URL pattern.
Find the product grid snippet (often main-collection-product-grid.liquid) and remove every within_collection instance.
Add a metafield definition storing each product's parent collection URL.
Edit the breadcrumb snippet to render from the metafield instead of the URL.
Publish on a duplicate theme first, verify, then push live.

test.method: Recrawl the site and confirm collection-path product URLs are gone and breadcrumbs still render correctly.

title: Merge low-demand product variants and canonicalize any variant pages you keep
hypothesis: If colour or size variants with no separate search demand are merged into native product options instead of separate pages, then the catalog stops splitting ranking signal across near-identical URLs.

signal.check: Separate pages exist for product variants (colour, size, material) with no individual search volume.

risk.note: Merging pages changes URLs; add 301 redirects to avoid losing existing rankings.

prerequisites: Variant search volume from a keyword tool
steps: Check search volume for each variant's exact name.
Merge variants with no separate demand into native Shopify variant options on 1 product page.
For any variant page kept because it has real demand, canonicalize it to the primary product via a metafield-driven tag.
Add 301 redirects from any merged variant URL to the primary product.

test.method: Check combined rankings and traffic on the merged product page versus the sum of the old variant pages.

title: Scale the main menu to the catalog and feature high-volume collections on the homepage
hypothesis: If the main menu exposes subcategories directly and the homepage features the highest-volume collections, then those collections rank better because the homepage holds the most internal links of any page on the site.

signal.check: High-volume collections are buried several clicks deep with no menu or homepage link.

risk.note: Navigation and homepage layout change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Volume ranking of all collections
steps: Rank collections by search volume.
Expose the top collections directly in the main menu instead of nesting them.
Feature the highest-volume collections on the homepage with a direct link.
Minimize the number of clicks from the homepage to any product.

test.method: Track ranking and clicks for the featured collections before and after the menu and homepage change.

title: Keep URLs short and keyword-bearing, and 301-redirect every URL change
hypothesis: If every URL is short, readable and keyword-bearing, and every URL change carries a 301 redirect, then rankings survive URL edits because the old address still resolves to the new one instead of returning a 404.

signal.check: URLs contain filler words, CMS-generated strings, or a handle was recently changed without confirming a redirect.

risk.note: Always confirm the redirect checkbox before saving a handle change, or the old URL 404s.

prerequisites: Edit access to page handles
steps: Strip filler words from any new or changed URL handle.
Confirm the platform's "create a redirect" checkbox is ticked before saving any handle change.
Avoid CMS-generated ID strings in URLs.
Spot-check old URLs after a change to confirm they 301 instead of 404.

test.method: Crawl the site after any batch of URL changes and confirm 0 broken old URLs.
test.read_point: after every batch of URL changes

title: Build hub-and-spoke internal links from body copy, not just the menu
hypothesis: If every supporting page links to its collection hub and to at least 1 sibling from within body copy, then the hub page accumulates authority faster because links buried only in the menu or footer carry less contextual weight.

signal.check: Content pages link to the hub collection only through the site menu, with no contextual body-copy links.

risk.note: Adding links only, easy to remove.

prerequisites: Site architecture spec with hub and spoke pages identified
steps: For each collection hub, list the spokes (products, posts) that should link to it.
Add a contextual body-copy link to the hub within the first 100 to 200 words of each spoke.
Add 3 to 5 links between sibling spokes using 2 to 4 word descriptive anchors, never "click here" or the brand name.
Use Search Console's Links report to find the most-linked pages and add links from them to priority pages.

test.method: Recrawl and confirm no orphan pages remain; track hub page ranking after the link additions.

title: Add an outbound citation and a money-page link to every content page
hypothesis: If every blog post or guide carries an outbound citation for its factual claims and an internal link to the money page it supports, then content pages stop being dead ends because a post with no internal links is a room without doors.

signal.check: A published blog post or guide has no outbound citation for its claims or no internal link to a money page.

prerequisites: Content inventory to audit
steps: Read each content page and check every factual claim has a citation.
Add an internal link to the money page it is meant to support.
Add a link from the money page back to its best 1 or 2 supporting posts.
Flag any post with no clear money page to support for a decision (merge, redirect or keep as pure informational).

test.method: Audit content pages quarterly for citation and money-page link coverage.

title: Add breadcrumbs, category tag links and a related-products module to product pages
hypothesis: If every product page carries breadcrumbs, tag-style category links and a related-products module, then both crawlers and shoppers find more of the catalog because the product page stops being a dead end.

signal.check: Product pages are missing breadcrumbs, category tag links or a related-products section.

prerequisites: Product template edit access
A related-products logic (by technique, use case or category)
steps: Add breadcrumbs sourced from the correct parent collection (after the R42/SEO-041 URL fix).
Add tag-style links to related categories on the product page.
Add a related-products module linking by real similarity (technique, use case), not just random picks.
Verify the new links appear in the page's initial HTML.

test.method: Track units per order and internal click-through from product pages before and after adding the modules.

title: Find and fix every orphan page with no internal link
hypothesis: If every page meant to be indexed gets at least 1 internal link from a crawlable page, then those pages have a real chance to rank because "Discovered, currently not indexed" often clears once internal links from stronger pages point to them.

signal.check: A crawl report shows pages with 0 internal links pointing to them.

prerequisites: A crawl report with an orphan-page list
steps: Run a crawl and pull the orphan-page report.
Add each wanted orphan page to the menu or link it from a relevant article or collection.
Recrawl to confirm the orphan count drops.
Check the Pages report for "Discovered, currently not indexed" pages clearing after the links are added.

test.method: Compare indexed status for the fixed pages 2 to 4 weeks after adding links.

title: Keep a ranking discontinued product page live with a shop-similar option instead of deleting it
hypothesis: If a discontinued or out-of-stock product page that still has rankings or traffic is kept live with the buy button swapped for "shop similar" or "notify me", then that traffic is not lost because deleting the page throws away an asset that still earns clicks.

signal.check: A discontinued or out-of-stock product with rankings or organic traffic has been deleted instead of kept live with an alternative call to action.

risk.note: Page stays live, CTA swap is easy to revert.

prerequisites: A list of discontinued or out-of-stock products with their traffic and rank
steps: Check Search Console traffic and rank for every discontinued or out-of-stock product before deleting anything.
For any page with real traffic or rank, keep it live and swap the buy button for "shop similar" or "notify me".
Only delete pages with no meaningful traffic or rank, and 301 them to the nearest relevant product or collection, never to an unrelated page or the homepage as a first resort.

test.method: Track traffic on kept pages versus what would have been lost if deleted.

title: Redirect a deleted product to its nearest relevant page, never to an unrelated one or the homepage by default
hypothesis: If a deleted product is redirected only to its nearest relevant product or collection, then visitors following an old link still land somewhere useful because sending an iPhone page's traffic to a perfume collection wastes both the click and the redirect.

signal.check: A deleted product's redirect points to an unrelated collection or defaults to the homepage.

risk.note: Redirect target can be changed at any time.

prerequisites: A record of the deleted product's category
steps: Before deleting a product, record its category and closest current substitute.
Add a 301 redirect to the nearest relevant product or collection.
Only fall back to the homepage when no relevant page exists.
Audit existing redirects for any that point to unrelated pages or default to the homepage.

test.method: Check bounce rate on redirected URLs before and after correcting the target.

title: Cap and justify any templated set of near-duplicate pages before scaling it
hypothesis: If every templated page (variant, location or attribute page) reused from 1 layout has its own demand, its own copy and a stated count cap, then the site avoids doorway-page risk because reusing a layout with no unique content across hundreds of pages reads as manipulative to Google.

signal.check: A templated page set (variant pages, location pages, attribute pages) is being scaled with no per-page demand check or a stated cap on how many will exist.

risk.note: A doorway-flagged batch can be pruned or merged, but ranking loss on affected pages may take time to recover.

prerequisites: Demand data for each templated page candidate
steps: Check search demand for each candidate templated page before publishing it.
Write unique copy for every page kept; do not repeat the same paragraph across pages.
Set and write down a maximum page count for the set, with the reason.
Ramp releases over time rather than publishing the whole set at once.

test.method: Monitor rankings across the templated set for a sitewide drop that would signal a doorway-page penalty.
test.read_point: monthly while the set is live

title: Batch-process a seasonal SKU turnover through the redirect-or-keep-live decision in 1 pass
hypothesis: If a whole batch of seasonal SKUs turning over at once is routed through the keep-live-or-redirect decision together, and the collection page and internal links are updated at the same time, then the seasonal transition takes 1 coordinated pass instead of leaving stragglers fixed product by product.

signal.check: A season just ended or is about to end and several SKUs are turning over without a single coordinated review.

prerequisites: A list of the season's turning-over SKUs
SEO-049 and SEO-050 decision rules in place
steps: List every SKU turning over for the season in 1 sheet.
Apply the keep-live or redirect decision to the whole batch in 1 pass.
Update the parent collection page and its internal links at the same time.
Confirm no dead links remain to any SKU that changed.

test.method: Check for 404s or stale links to turned-over SKUs right after the batch pass.

title: Fix Shopify's product URL duplication before deploying a custom robots.txt
hypothesis: If the product URL duplication fix and breadcrumb rebuild happen before a custom robots.txt is deployed, then the robots.txt correctly blocks the intended page classes because deploying it first can lock in the wrong duplicate-path assumptions.

signal.check: A custom robots.txt is being planned or was deployed before the product URL duplication fix (SEO-041) was live.

prerequisites: SEO-041 (URL duplication fix) confirmed live
steps: Confirm the product URL duplication fix and breadcrumb rebuild are live and verified.
Only then add the robots.txt.liquid template with the intended disallow rules.
Keep the Sitemap line in the new robots.txt.
Recheck after any app install, since apps can silently edit robots.txt.

test.method: Crawl the site after deployment and confirm no wanted page is blocked and no duplicate path is missed.
test.read_point: immediately after deployment, then after every app install

title: Set the collection title tag, H1 and URL to the target keyword
hypothesis: If a collection's title tag leads with the keyword at about 60 characters, its H1 equals the keyword, and its URL mirrors it, then the page communicates its topic clearly to both Google and shoppers scanning the search result.

signal.check: A collection's title tag buries the keyword after modifiers, its H1 is vague, or its URL does not mirror the keyword.

risk.note: Copy and handle edit, keep the redirect if the URL changes.

prerequisites: Confirmed target keyword for the collection
steps: Put the keyword first in the title tag, about 60 characters, modifiers after.
Set the H1 to the exact target keyword.
Shorten the URL handle to mirror the keyword, removing filler words.
Tick the redirect option if the handle changes.

test.method: Check CTR and position for the collection's target query before and after the change.

title: Add a real description above and below the collection grid, not a bare grid
hypothesis: If a collection page carries a short description above the grid and a 400 to 1,000 word description below it for a contested term, then the page has a real chance to rank because a bare H1 plus grid gives Google nothing to understand the page by.

signal.check: A collection page competing for a real term shows only a grid with little or no description text.

risk.note: Copy addition, keep prior version saved.

prerequisites: A way to split the description above and below the grid (a marker snippet or read-more toggle)
steps: Write up to 2 lines above the grid explaining what the collection is and for whom.
Write 400 to 1,000 words below the grid for a contested term (at least 100 words for any collection).
Add contextual links to subcollections and related guides within the description.
Avoid keyword stuffing; write for the shopper deciding, not for a word count.

test.method: Compare ranking and clicks for the collection before and after adding the description.

title: Fix the collection grid to 36 to 48 products, numbered pagination and no JavaScript rendering
hypothesis: If the collection grid shows 36 to 48 products with numbered pagination rendered in server HTML, then the page crawls and browses cleanly because a JavaScript-only grid or infinite scroll can hide products from crawlers and from shoppers using pagination.

signal.check: The collection grid is rendered by JavaScript, uses only previous/next navigation, or shows an unusual product count per page.

risk.note: Switching grid apps can change layout; test on a duplicate theme first.

prerequisites: Shopify's native Search and Discovery app or an equivalent server-rendered grid
steps: Switch to a native, server-rendered grid app instead of a JavaScript grid.
Set the grid to show 36 to 48 products per page.
Use numbered pagination instead of previous/next only.
Show colour, a short spec and price on each tile.

test.method: Crawl the collection with JavaScript off to confirm all products appear in the HTML.
test.read_point: immediately after the change, then next full crawl

title: Add a real FAQ accordion and 3 genuine featured reviews to competing collection pages
hypothesis: If a collection page adds an FAQ built from real People Also Ask questions and 3 hand-picked, genuine reviews mentioning the keyword, then shoppers get answers and trust signals in plain HTML because rich-result payoff for FAQ schema is declining and the value now comes from the content itself, not the snippet.

signal.check: A competing collection page has no FAQ section and no featured reviews on the page.

risk.note: Content addition only; reviews must be genuine and unincentivised.

prerequisites: Real People Also Ask questions for the keyword
Genuine unincentivised reviews mentioning the keyword
steps: Pull real People Also Ask questions for the collection's target keyword.
Build an FAQ accordion from these questions in plain HTML.
Select 3 genuine reviews that mention the keyword and feature them on the page.
Do not offer any incentive for the reviews used.

test.method: Track conversion rate on the collection page before and after adding FAQ and reviews.

title: Rewrite search engine listings for clicks, not just keywords
lever: meta title and description for CTR
hypothesis: If every indexable page's title carries a call to action or differentiator and its meta description says what the shopper gets in 150 to 160 characters, then click-through rate improves because the meta description does not affect ranking, only whether someone clicks.

signal.check: A page's search listing is a bare keyword with no CTA, differentiator or benefit statement, or the meta description is missing.

prerequisites: List of pages with weak or missing meta titles and descriptions
steps: Rewrite the title to include the keyword plus a call to action or differentiator (for example "buy natural soap online, fast delivery" instead of just "natural soap").
Write a 150 to 160 character meta description that ends with a clear benefit or CTA.
Check the rendered snippet in an incognito search after publishing.

test.method: Compare CTR for the page's queries in Search Console before and after the rewrite, holding position steady.

title: Fix heading structure to exactly 1 H1 per page with sequential H2 and H3
hypothesis: If every template shows exactly 1 H1 and headings run sequentially from H2 to H3, then the page's topic is unambiguous because a custom section can silently add a second H1 or skip a heading level without anyone noticing.

signal.check: Inspecting a template shows 0 or 2 or more H1 tags, or a heading level is skipped (H2 straight to H4).

prerequisites: Inspect element access on home, collection, product and blog templates
steps: Inspect each template's headings for the home, collection, product and blog post.
Demote any second H1 (often from a custom section) to H2.
Fix any skipped heading level to run sequentially.
Use natural keyword phrasing in headings, not a repeated exact match.

test.method: Recheck heading structure on each template after the fix.
test.read_point: immediately after the fix, then each quarterly audit

title: Prioritize collection pages over product pages for a store with 50 or more SKUs
hypothesis: If a store with 50 or more products puts collection page optimization ahead of individual product pages, then organic revenue grows faster because collections likely carry most of the organic revenue on catalogs that size, even though product pages convert at a higher individual rate.
does_not_apply_when: The store has a hero-SKU or thin catalog under 50 products

signal.check: SEO time is split evenly or weighted toward product pages despite the store having 50 or more SKUs.

expected_effect.size: 1 agency reports collections driving over 80% of organic revenue on stores this size, an unaudited claim

risk.note: Prioritization only, product pages still get worked on afterward.

prerequisites: Confirmed catalog size of 50 or more products
steps: Confirm the catalog has 50 or more products.
Rank collection pages ahead of individual product pages in the work queue.
Track organic revenue split by template (collection vs product) once GA4 data allows it.
Revisit the priority if the data shows a different split for this store.

test.method: Track organic revenue by landing-page template over time to confirm or correct the assumed split.

title: Index a product page only when its name or attributes have real search volume
hypothesis: If a product page is optimized and indexed only when its name or attribute combination has real search volume, then SEO effort is not wasted on made-up product names because a page with no demand cannot rank no matter how well it is built.

signal.check: Products with invented or highly specific names (with no search volume) are being fully optimized for SEO the same way as high-demand products.

risk.note: Noindex can be reversed if demand changes later.

prerequisites: Search volume data for product names and attributes
steps: Check search volume for each product's exact name and key attribute combination.
For products with real volume, fully optimize and keep them indexed.
For products with no volume, put the SEO effort into the parent collection and consider noindexing the product page.
Record the decision on the keyword map or architecture spec.

test.method: Compare organic clicks on the parent collection versus the noindexed product pages over time.

title: Rewrite product titles the way a shopper actually searches, and use the title as the H1
hypothesis: If a product title is rewritten as a shopper would search it, with the main keyword and 1 supporting term, and used as both the title tag and H1, then the page has a real chance to rank because a cute internal name like "Sweet Honey Bomb" tells Google nothing about the product.

signal.check: Product titles use internal branding names with no descriptive keyword, or the H1 differs from the title tag.

risk.note: Title change only; keep the old title as an alt for internal reference if needed.

prerequisites: Confirmed product keyword from the keyword map
steps: Identify the descriptive keyword and supporting term for each product.
Rewrite the product title to include the product name as shoppers search it plus 1 supporting term.
Set the H1 to match the title.
For large catalogs, template the pattern (brand plus product plus 1 attribute) to bulk-apply it.

test.method: Track ranking and clicks for the product's target query before and after the title rewrite.

title: Build the full product content stack with explicit facts, not manufacturer copy
hypothesis: If a product page carries a short description, feature bullets, a spec table and a 300 to 1,000 word detailed description with explicit facts (size, colour, material, use case), then the page ranks and converts better because identical manufacturer copy across sellers decays in search value over time.

signal.check: A product page uses the manufacturer's supplied description word for word, or gives vague marketing phrases with no explicit facts.

risk.note: Copy rewrite, previous version can be restored.

prerequisites: Real product specs, materials and use cases
steps: Write a 50 to 150 word short description naming the product and its core benefit.
Add feature and benefit bullets plus a spec table (weight, size, material, capacity).
Write a 300 to 1,000 word detailed description with differentiators and explicit facts the manufacturer sheet does not include.
State size, colour, material and use case explicitly instead of vague marketing phrases.

test.method: Compare organic clicks and add-to-cart rate before and after replacing manufacturer copy.

title: Fix product image SEO: descriptive names, real alt text, compression and lazy-load rules
hypothesis: If every product image gets a descriptive file name, alt text naming the product and what the image shows, WebP or JPEG compression, and lazy-loading on everything except the main image, then image search traffic and page speed both improve because numbered file names and repeated alt phrases give search engines nothing to work with.

signal.check: Product images use numbered file names, repeated or missing alt text, or the main product image is set to lazy-load.

risk.note: Image metadata and compression changes only.

prerequisites: Real product photos for every SKU
steps: Rename image files descriptively (product name plus visual descriptor).
Write alt text describing the image with the product name and a visual descriptor, never repeated across many images.
Convert images to WebP or JPEG, compress and resize to display size.
Lazy-load every image except the main (LCP) product image.
Confirm every product image is included in the XML sitemap.

test.method: Check image search impressions and page weight before and after the fix.

title: Collect unincentivised post-purchase reviews and emit Review and AggregateRating schema
hypothesis: If reviews are collected by a plain post-purchase email request with no incentive, and the review app is verified to output Review and AggregateRating markup, then the product page earns star ratings in search results because incentivised reviews are against policy and unverified schema silently fails.

signal.check: Review requests offer a discount or incentive, or no one has verified that the review app's schema output actually validates.

risk.note: Review request wording change plus a schema check.

prerequisites: Post-purchase email flow
A review app on the store
steps: Send a plain post-purchase review request with no discount or incentive attached.
Confirm the review app actually emits Review and AggregateRating schema on the product page.
Validate the markup in the Rich Results Test.
Fix any missing or malformed schema field found.

test.method: Check Search Console's Shopping and Enhancements reports for schema errors and star-rating appearance in search results.
test.read_point: 4 to 8 weeks after fixing the schema

title: Implement and validate Product, Review, FAQ and Breadcrumb schema on every money page
hypothesis: If Product, Review or AggregateRating, FAQPage and BreadcrumbList schema are implemented and validated in 2 tools on every money page, then rich results appear reliably because a missing comma can silently cost the whole rich result and the theme's default markup is often incomplete.

signal.check: Money pages have not been checked in a structured data validator, or the theme's default schema has never been verified as complete.

risk.note: Schema deploy can be removed or reverted.

prerequisites: View-source access to check existing markup
steps: Inventory what schema the theme already emits on product, collection, article and breadcrumb templates.
Fill any gaps (Product with offers, AggregateRating, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, Article) matching visible facts.
Validate in the Rich Results Test and a second validator; they can disagree, so check both.
Watch Search Console's Shopping and Enhancements reports after the next crawl.

test.method: Recheck the Enhancements report for errors 2 to 4 weeks after fixing schema.

title: Deploy schema markup through Google Tag Manager when theme code access is unavailable
hypothesis: If Product, FAQ or Breadcrumb schema is deployed as a Custom HTML tag in Tag Manager with a Page Path trigger when theme access is missing, then structured data still ships because the schema does not require touching the theme's code at all.
does_not_apply_when: The agent already has direct theme code access

signal.check: Schema is needed on a page but no one has theme editing access, so structured data work is stalled.

risk.note: GTM misconfiguration can duplicate or break schema; preview before publishing.

prerequisites: Google Tag Manager already installed
Generated schema JSON-LD for the page
steps: Generate the schema JSON-LD in a schema generator tool.
Create a Custom HTML tag in Tag Manager containing the JSON-LD.
Set a Page View trigger with Page Path equal to the exact URL.
Preview the tag before publishing, then publish and validate live.

test.method: Validate the live page in the Rich Results Test after publishing the GTM tag.

title: Add first-hand experience signals to product and comparison pages
hypothesis: If money and comparison pages carry original photos, real screenshots or test notes, a named author, and publish and updated dates, then those pages carry more real credibility because generic content with no first-hand signal is easy for both shoppers and Google to discount.

signal.check: A page competing on a commercial or comparison term has no original photos, no named author and no visible dates.

prerequisites: Real product photos or test notes
A named author or expert at the brand
steps: Add original photos or screenshots taken by the team, not stock images.
Add a named author byline with a short credibility line.
Show a publish date and an updated date.
Use a consistent structure across every page in a comparison set.

test.method: Compare time on page and conversion for pages with these signals versus generic pages.

title: Render reviews, FAQs and specs in server HTML, not injected later by a JavaScript widget
hypothesis: If reviews, FAQs and specs load in the initial server HTML instead of being injected after load by an app widget, then more crawlers and AI engines can read them because most crawlers only see load-time HTML.

signal.check: Disabling JavaScript and reloading a product page hides the reviews, FAQ or spec table, showing only placeholders.

risk.note: May require a different app or a server-side rendering configuration; test on a duplicate theme first.

prerequisites: A JavaScript-off testing method (browser extension or dev tools)
steps: Disable JavaScript and reload the product and collection templates.
Note which sections (reviews, FAQ, spec table) disappear or show placeholders.
Switch to a server-rendering app or configuration for those sections.
Recheck with JavaScript off to confirm the content now appears.

test.method: Check the URL Inspection rendered HTML in Search Console after the fix.
test.read_point: after the fix, then each quarterly audit

title: Use only real product photos on product and collection pages, save stock or generated images for blog posts
hypothesis: If product and collection pages use only real photos of the actual product, and stock or generated images are limited to purely informational blog posts, then shoppers trust the page more because a redrawn or stock image standing in for the real product misleads on accuracy.

signal.check: A product or collection page shows a stock photo or an AI-generated image instead of a real photo of the product.

prerequisites: Real product photography for the affected SKUs
steps: Audit product and collection pages for any stock or generated image standing in for the real product.
Replace with real photos where accuracy matters.
Reserve stock or generated images for illustrative use on informational blog posts only.
Never use a generated image that redraws the actual product being sold.

test.method: Compare conversion and return rate before and after replacing stand-in images with real photos.

title: Build a dedicated page template for subscription products with cadence, pause and price-per-delivery
hypothesis: If a subscription product's cadence, pause and cancel terms and price-per-delivery are stated on the page itself instead of only at checkout, then shoppers convert with fewer support questions because they know the commitment before they buy.

signal.check: A subscription product page shows only a single price with no cadence, pause, cancel or per-delivery pricing detail.

prerequisites: The subscription terms (cadence options, pause and cancel policy, per-delivery price)
steps: State the delivery cadence options clearly on the product page.
State the pause and cancel terms in plain language on the page, not only at checkout.
Show price-per-delivery alongside any bundled or discounted price.
Treat this as its own template, separate from a one-off product page.

test.method: Compare add-to-cart rate and post-purchase support tickets about cadence or cancellation before and after the change.

title: Give every bundle or kit its own product page with its own keyword and spec table
hypothesis: If a bundle or kit gets its own product page with its own keyword, price and spec table instead of being folded into a single component's page or an upsell widget, then it can rank for its own search demand and clearly show shoppers what is included.

signal.check: A bundle or kit exists only as an upsell widget or a variant of a single product, with no standalone page.

risk.note: New page addition, does not remove the individual component pages.

prerequisites: A defined bundle or kit with its own SKU
steps: Check search volume for the bundle or kit's likely name.
Create a standalone product page with its own title, keyword and URL.
Add a spec table listing every item included and the combined price versus buying separately.
Link the bundle page from each component product page.

test.method: Track organic clicks and AOV contribution from the standalone bundle page.

title: Only blog in buyer-intent formats that support a collection, not generic lifestyle posts
hypothesis: If the blog only publishes buyer-intent formats (versus, alternatives, best-for-use-case, buying guide) that link into a collection, then blog traffic actually supports organic revenue because generic seasonal and lifestyle posts rarely rank or convert.
does_not_apply_when: The store has no money pages built yet to support

signal.check: Blog posts are being planned or published in generic seasonal or lifestyle formats with no link into a collection they support.

expected_effect.size: 1 case's 210 posts drove under 7% of traffic directly but supported collection rankings; another store's blog drove over half its organic traffic

prerequisites: Money pages already built (SEO-004)
steps: Screen every planned blog topic against the 4 buyer-intent formats: versus, alternatives, best-for-use-case, buying guide.
Reject generic seasonal or lifestyle topics with no path to a collection.
Link every kept post to the collection or product it is meant to support.
Measure blog pages on assisted organic revenue, not raw traffic.

test.method: Track assisted conversions from blog landing pages against the collections they support.

title: Build 1 cluster of 5 to 10 pieces around 1 money page before starting the next
hypothesis: If content is built as 1 full cluster of 5 to 10 pieces around 1 money page before starting the next cluster, then each money page gets a real chance to rank because splitting effort across many half-built clusters dilutes the internal linking and topical authority that a finished cluster provides.

signal.check: Several content clusters are in progress at once with none finished, or fewer than 5 pieces exist around any given money page.

prerequisites: 1 money page already optimized (SEO-004)
steps: Pick 1 money page and list every angle a buyer searches around it (definitions, how-to, comparisons, alternatives, buying guide).
Produce and publish 5 to 10 pieces for that cluster before starting the next money page's cluster.
Link every piece to the money page and to its siblings.
Publish a bridge post (a versus-style comparison) when moving to the next cluster.

test.method: Track organic clicks for the money page and its cluster once all pieces are live.
test.read_point: 3 to 6 months after the cluster is complete

title: Write factual comparison and alternatives content that names competitors directly
hypothesis: If comparison and alternatives content is factual, names 7 to 10 real competitors, and puts the store's own brand first with claims it can support, then the store wins the comparison search instead of ceding it to competitors or an AI summary.

signal.check: The store has no comparison or alternatives content for its category, or existing comparison content avoids naming any real competitor.

expected_effect.size: one case ranked number 3 for a competitor's brand name within about a week, self-reported

risk.note: Never write hostile or unsupported claims about a named competitor; keep it factual to avoid disputes.

prerequisites: Accurate, defensible facts about the store's own product and named competitors
steps: Pick a comparison term worth targeting (brand vs brand, or best alternatives to X).
