List 7 to 10 real competitors and their real, checkable attributes.
Put the store's own product first with claims it can support.
Never write hostile or unverifiable claims about a competitor.

test.method: Track ranking and clicks for the comparison term after publishing.

title: Read the top 5 ranking pages and add what a shopper needs to decide that they skip
hypothesis: If a new page reads the top 5 ranking results for its keyword and adds specs, comparisons or real photos those pages skip, then it earns the click because Google rewards completeness, not word count, and simply lengthening a page does not add real value.

signal.check: A new page is being written without first reading and recording table stakes and gaps from the top 5 current results.

expected_effect.size: unknown; over 96% of pages get no Google traffic per a secondhand Ahrefs figure

prerequisites: P5 SERP check already run for the target keyword
steps: Read the top 5 ranking pages in full for the target keyword.
Record table stakes (what every result covers), gaps (what none cover) and average length.
Write the new page to cover the table stakes plus fill the gap with real specs, comparisons or photos.
Do not pad length just to match or exceed the top results' word count.

test.method: Track ranking against the top 5 after publishing.

title: Build the store's real moat: testing notes, real customer photos and sizing data
hypothesis: If money pages carry the store's own product testing notes, real customer photos, sizing and fit data, and return-rate-informed advice instead of generic expert quotes, then the content is harder to copy because it comes from data only this store has.

signal.check: A money or comparison page relies on generic expert quotes or manufacturer facts with no store-specific testing, photo or return data.

prerequisites: Internal testing notes or return-rate data
Real customer photos
steps: Pull the store's own testing notes, fit feedback and return-rate data for the product.
Add real customer photos where available.
Write sizing or fit guidance based on this data, not generic advice.
Treat this as non-negotiable for health, money or safety-related topics.

test.method: Track return rate and conversion for pages with this content versus generic pages.

title: Go deeper than the AI Overview for any query that triggers one
hypothesis: If a page adds original data, hands-on notes and the follow-up questions a buyer has after reading an AI Overview, then it earns the click because a page that only restates the AI summary gives no reason to visit it.

signal.check: A target query shows an AI Overview and the current or planned page only restates the same summary points.

prerequisites: The AI Overview text for the target query
steps: Read the AI Overview for the target query and list what it covers.
Add original data, hands-on notes, specific products, prices and dimensions the summary lacks.
Answer the follow-up questions a buyer likely has after reading the summary.
Mark the term as an AI-visibility target on the keyword map.

test.method: Track clicks on the query after the page is updated to go beyond the AI Overview.

title: Refresh a page-2-or-3 or CTR-falling page before writing anything new
hypothesis: If a page on page 2 or 3, or one losing CTR at a stable position, is refreshed before any new page is written, then the fastest available win is taken first because updating an existing near-ranking page usually beats starting from zero.

signal.check: A page sits at positions 4 to 30 with real impressions, or its CTR is falling at a stable position, and no refresh has been scheduled.

risk.note: Save the previous copy before editing so it can be restored.

prerequisites: Search Console position and CTR data by page
steps: Pull pages at positions 4 to 30 with impressions, plus any with falling CTR at a stable position.
Compare the target keyword with the page's actual click leader; retarget title and H1 if they differ.
Re-run the SERP check; add missing subtopics, data and first-hand notes; update the year in the title if present.
Fix internal links to and from the page, then request indexing.

test.method: Compare clicks, impressions, CTR and position 4 to 8 weeks after the refresh against the pre-change window.

title: Publish on a steady cadence the team can review, and ramp bulk releases instead of flooding
hypothesis: If content is published on a fixed, human-reviewable cadence and any bulk release is ramped up gradually instead of flooded, then quality holds steady because no source procedure allows publishing faster than a person can check.

signal.check: Content is published in irregular bursts with no fixed cadence, or a bulk batch is planned to go live all at once.

prerequisites: A content calendar
steps: Set a fixed minimum cadence (at least 2 posts a month) the team can actually review.
For any bulk release (many templated or programmatic pages), ramp the count up over days instead of publishing all at once.
Cap the pace at what a human can quality-check before it goes live.

test.method: Track quality-gate pass rate and any ranking volatility after adopting the cadence.

title: Syndicate content only as a rewritten variant, with the original kept canonical on the store
hypothesis: If any syndicated version of a post (LinkedIn, a partner site) is rewritten rather than identical, and the original stays canonical on the store, then the store keeps the ranking value of its own content because republishing identical articles across sites risks a duplicate-content penalty.

signal.check: A post has been republished identically on another platform with no rewrite and no canonical pointing back to the store.

risk.note: Republished copy can be edited or removed.

prerequisites: A disclosed brand channel to syndicate to (LinkedIn company page, a named partner)
steps: Rewrite the post as a genuine variant for the syndication channel, not a copy-paste.
Keep the original on the store marked canonical.
Only syndicate to disclosed brand channels, never to an undisclosed third-party site posing as editorial content.
Have staff share the syndicated variant to build its own reach.

test.method: Check that the original page's ranking holds steady after syndication.

title: Build 1 simple linkable asset per category when an easy content gap exists
hypothesis: If the store builds 1 simple linkable asset (a calculator, a definitive guide, original data) per category once money pages and the first cluster are done, then it earns links more easily because a useful tool attracts links content alone usually cannot.

signal.check: The category has no calculator, comparison tool or original-data asset that other sites might want to link to.

expected_effect.size: one example built a simple calculator at about 500 searches and low difficulty in about 10 minutes with an AI coding tool

prerequisites: Money pages and first content cluster already built (SEO-004, SEO-074)
steps: Identify a simple, useful tool or data gap in the category (a calculator, a comparison table, a sizing tool).
Build the simplest version that answers the real need.
Publish it and link it from the relevant money page and cluster.
Note that content-only link earning is slow and works best for already high-authority brands; a linkable asset speeds it up for smaller stores.

test.method: Track referring domains and links to the asset over time.

title: Build comparison and trust content earlier for a considered-purchase or high-AOV store
hypothesis: If a low-frequency, high-AOV or considered-purchase store builds its comparison, guarantee, sizing and alternatives content earlier in the plan, then conversion improves because these buyers research longer before they buy and need that trust layer sooner than a low-AOV, impulse buyer would.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells low-AOV, impulse-purchase products where buyers convert with little research

signal.check: A high-AOV or considered-purchase store's content plan puts comparison, guarantee and sizing content late, after basic money pages, the same as a low-AOV plan would.

prerequisites: Money pages for the considered-purchase product already live
steps: Confirm the product is a high-AOV or considered purchase with a longer research cycle.
Move reviews, guarantees, sizing or fit guides and alternatives pages earlier in the content sequence.
Build these ahead of lower-priority informational content.
Track whether shoppers reach these pages before converting.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for sessions that visited trust content before purchase versus those that did not.
test.read_point: 8 to 12 weeks after publishing the trust content

title: Write a structured page brief before producing any content piece
hypothesis: If every content piece starts from a written brief (terms, SERP structure, table stakes, the gap to fill, links, moat items, sources) instead of a blank page, then output stays consistent because the writer or AI tool has a checklist instead of guessing what the page needs.

signal.check: Content is being produced without a written brief covering terms, SERP structure and required links.

prerequisites: The cluster's money page and the SERP check for the target keyword (SEO-017)
steps: For each piece, write the primary and secondary terms, the SERP's dominant format and table stakes from the top 5.
Name the specific gap this piece will fill and the money page it supports.
List required sibling links, human-moat items, cited sources and needed real images.
Hand the brief to the writer or AI drafting step before any copy is produced.

test.method: Compare the revision count and quality-gate pass rate for briefed pieces versus unbriefed ones.
test.read_point: after each content cluster is complete

title: Ground every AI-assisted product or collection draft in the real catalog feed and existing reviews
hypothesis: If an AI draft for a product or collection page is fed the actual catalog data, real specs and existing reviews for that SKU instead of a generic brand-voice prompt alone, then fewer weak ideas make it into the draft because the model is grounded in real product facts, not invented ones.

signal.check: An AI content prompt for a product or collection page includes no real catalog data, specs or reviews for that specific SKU.

expected_effect.size: one source pastes the category page plus 5 product pages as sources and still expects about 20% weak ideas

prerequisites: Brand voice document and banned-word list
Real specs and reviews for the SKU
steps: Assemble the category page, several product pages, real specs and existing reviews for the SKU.
Feed these plus the brand voice document into the AI drafting prompt.
Ask the model clarifying questions before it writes, and answer them.
Expect and budget time to remove about 20% weak ideas from the output.

test.method: Track the share of AI-drafted content kept versus rewritten across a batch of pages.

title: Run every AI-assisted draft through outline approval, fact-check and a human rewrite pass before publishing
hypothesis: If every AI-assisted page passes outline approval, a fact-check against brand data, and a hand rewrite of the weakest 10 to 20 percent before publishing, then AI-assisted content reaches the same quality bar as hand-written content because the draft never goes live without a human checking it.

signal.check: AI-generated drafts are published or scheduled without an outline approval step, a fact-check pass, or any hand rewrite.

risk.note: Process gate only; nothing publishes without it.

prerequisites: A grounded AI draft (SEO-085)
The page brief (SEO-084)
steps: Approve the outline first and reject any section the store cannot actually deliver on.
Generate the full draft into a document, not directly into the CMS.
Fact-check every number, claim and product detail against real brand data.
Add first-hand moat details by hand and rewrite the weakest 10 to 20 percent.
Run the reading-level and claims gate, then publish only as a draft for a person to schedule.

test.method: Track how many published AI-assisted pages needed a correction after going live, before and after adding the gate.

title: Fix the 4-item technical floor before chasing any other SEO work
hypothesis: If every money page is crawlable and indexed, has no broken links, works on mobile checkout and PDP, and sits in a clear category hierarchy, then content and link work can actually pay off because a blocked money page beats any content or link gain.

signal.check: No one has confirmed all money pages are crawlable, indexed, free of broken links, and usable on mobile.

risk.note: Diagnostic and fix pass; each fix is independently reversible.

prerequisites: A crawler and Search Console access
steps: Confirm every collection and product meant to sell is crawlable and indexed.
Fix any broken links pointing to product pages.
Check mobile checkout and PDP usability on a real phone.
Confirm the category hierarchy is clear from home to product.
Do not go further into technical depth than these 4 items before pages exist and are optimized.

test.method: Recheck the 4-item floor after fixes and track indexed money-page count.
test.read_point: 1 to 2 weeks after fixes, then quarterly

title: Crawl the whole site with mobile and JavaScript rendering, fix errors first
hypothesis: If the whole site is crawled with a mobile user agent and JavaScript rendering, and errors are fixed before warnings and notices, then real problems get fixed first because a high health score can still hide 404s, canonical mismatches and orphan pages.

signal.check: The site has not had a full crawl in the last quarter, or the last crawl's errors were not worked before warnings and notices.

expected_effect.size: one audit showed a health score of 96 out of 100 while 404s, canonical mismatches, orphan pages and oversized images were still present

risk.note: Diagnostic pass, fixes applied one at a time.

prerequisites: A crawler (Screaming Frog free to 500 URLs, Sitebulb, or Semrush Site Audit)
steps: Set the crawler to mobile user agent with JavaScript rendering and structured-data checks on.
Work errors first: 404s, canonical mismatches, orphan pages, http links, missing titles or H1s.
Work warnings second, notices last.
Do not chase a perfect health score; reduce the real error count instead.

test.method: Recrawl after fixes and compare error count.

title: Apply the "do I want this on Google" test before fixing any not-indexed page
hypothesis: If every not-indexed page is checked with "do I want people to find this on Google" before anyone touches it, then effort only goes toward real problems because cart, checkout, thank-you, staging and filtered pages are supposed to be excluded, and fixing them wastes time.

signal.check: The not-indexed report has not been reviewed to separate intentional exclusions from real problems.

prerequisites: Search Console Pages report grouped by reason
steps: Open the Pages report grouped by not-indexed reason.
Mark cart, checkout, account, internal search, filtered pages, thank-you and staging as intentional.
Flag any money page in the excluded group as a real problem.
Fix only the unintended exclusions: remove the noindex tag or robots block and resubmit.

test.method: Recheck the Pages report after fixes to confirm money pages moved out of the excluded group.

title: Read the URL Inspection reason before acting on a page that will not appear
hypothesis: If the URL Inspection reason is read before acting on a page that should rank but does not, then the right fix gets applied because "Discovered, currently not indexed" needs internal links and patience while "Crawled, currently not indexed" often needs a stronger page or more sitewide authority, not endless rewriting.

signal.check: A page that should rank is being rewritten repeatedly with no one checking its URL Inspection status reason first.

prerequisites: Search Console URL Inspection access
steps: Run URL Inspection on the page that should rank but does not appear.
If "Discovered, currently not indexed": add internal links from stronger pages and wait.
If "Crawled, currently not indexed" on a small or new site: focus on sitewide authority instead of rewriting the page again.
Only request indexing after applying the matching fix.

test.method: Recheck the page's index status 2 to 4 weeks after the matching fix.

title: Request indexing only after a fix is live, respecting the daily quota
hypothesis: If indexing is requested only after a page's fix has gone live, spaced within the daily quota, then requests are not wasted on pages that will just be re-crawled unchanged and flagged again.

signal.check: Indexing requests are being sent before a fix is confirmed live, or many requests are sent in a single day well past a sensible daily limit.

prerequisites: Search Console access
steps: Confirm the fix (content, noindex removal, redirect) is live before requesting indexing.
Spread requests across days instead of batching them all at once, respecting the quota.
Log which pages were requested and when.

test.method: Track how many requested pages actually get re-crawled and re-indexed within a few days.

title: Fix canonical tags so every page has exactly 1 live canonical, never a redirect
hypothesis: If every page's canonical points to its own live final URL, never to a redirect or a different collection path, then ranking signal is not split or lost because a canonical pointing at a redirect is a bug that confuses which URL should rank.

signal.check: A crawler's canonical report shows a canonical pointing to a redirect, missing, or pointing at the wrong collection path.

prerequisites: Crawler canonical report
steps: Pull the canonical report from the site crawl.
Fix any canonical pointing to a redirect to point at the live final URL instead.
Set variant page canonicals through a metafield to their primary product.
Recrawl to confirm every page self-references or points to its correct primary variant.

test.method: Recrawl and confirm 0 canonicals point to a redirect.

title: 301-redirect every dead URL to its nearest relevant page and update internal links
hypothesis: If every dead URL from a deletion, migration or URL change gets a 301 to the nearest relevant page and internal links are updated to the final https URL, then link equity and visitor traffic are not lost to a 404 or a redirect chain.

signal.check: A crawl shows internal links pointing to 404s, redirect chains, or http URLs instead of the final https destination.

risk.note: Redirects can be edited or removed.

prerequisites: Crawl report of 404s and redirect chains
steps: Pull every 404 and its internal links from the crawl.
Add a 301 redirect from each dead URL to the nearest relevant page.
Update internal links to point straight to the final https URL instead of relying on the redirect.
Recrawl to confirm the old URL no longer returns 404.

test.method: Recrawl and confirm 0 internal links point to 404s or redirect chains.

title: Fix the sitemap: primary domain, submission, product images, correct exclusions
hypothesis: If the sitemap is checked against the confirmed primary domain, submitted in Search Console, includes product images, and excludes noindexed pages through theme code rather than a toggle that also forces noindex, then Google gets an accurate map of what to crawl.

signal.check: The sitemap was submitted before the primary domain was set, is missing product images, or noindexed pages are still listed in it.

prerequisites: Confirmed custom primary domain
steps: Confirm the custom domain is set as primary before touching the sitemap.
Open /sitemap.xml and submit it under Search Console's Sitemaps.
Reference the sitemap in robots.txt.
Confirm product images are included, and use theme code (not the hidden Shopify toggle) to exclude noindexed pages so they are not also force-nofollowed.
Ignore the priority attribute; it is not used by Google.

test.method: Check the Sitemaps report for a "success" status and confirm excluded URLs are absent.

title: Fix robots.txt to block low-value paths without accidentally blocking a wanted page or an AI crawler
hypothesis: If robots.txt blocks admin, cart, checkout, account, internal search and low-value filter paths while keeping a Sitemap line and never blocking a wanted page or crawler, then crawl budget goes to real pages because robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing, and a wrong rule can hide a whole page class from Google or an AI engine.

signal.check: robots.txt has never been reviewed for accidental blocks, or an app installed since the last check may have edited it.

risk.note: A wrong disallow rule can hide an entire page class; test with a curl check before and after any change.

prerequisites: Access to edit robots.txt (theme code on Shopify)
steps: Open /robots.txt and list every disallow rule.
Confirm admin, cart, checkout, account, internal search and low-value filter paths are blocked.
Confirm no wanted money page is blocked and the Sitemap line is present.
Test with `curl -A ClaudeBot yourdomain.com` and similar for other AI crawlers to confirm they are allowed or blocked on purpose.
Recheck robots.txt after every app install, since apps can edit it silently.

test.method: Recrawl and confirm no wanted page is blocked; repeat the curl checks after each app install.
test.read_point: immediately after any change, then after every app install

title: Put money-page content in the initial HTML and test with JavaScript off
hypothesis: If money-page content (title, description, reviews, FAQ, specs) loads in the initial HTML and is tested with JavaScript disabled, then more crawlers and AI engines see the full page because most AI crawlers do not render JavaScript even though Google can.

signal.check: A money page has not been tested with JavaScript disabled to confirm its core content still appears.

risk.note: Diagnostic test; any resulting fix is independently reversible.

prerequisites: A way to disable JavaScript in the browser
steps: Disable JavaScript and reload each money page template.
Confirm title, description, reviews, FAQ and specs are all visible without JavaScript.
Fix any section that only appears after a script runs.
Check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection as a second confirmation.

test.method: Repeat the JavaScript-off test after any theme or app change that touches these templates.
test.read_point: after every theme or app change touching these templates

title: Move any video meant to earn video search results onto its own watch page
hypothesis: If a product or how-to video is the main content of its own page, above the fold, then it can earn video search results because a video embedded mid-post ranks as a normal page with no video-specific feature.

signal.check: Search Console's Videos report shows "Video isn't on a watch page" for a video the store wants in video results.

risk.note: New page or template change, does not remove existing embeds.

prerequisites: A video the store wants to rank in video results
steps: Identify any video the store wants to appear in video search results.
Move it to its own page as the main content, placed above the fold.
Keep the mid-post embed elsewhere as a normal page element, not the video's primary home.
Check the Videos report for the fix.

test.method: Recheck the Videos report a few weeks after moving the video to its own watch page.

title: Use a Search Console Domain property to cover every subdomain and protocol variant
hypothesis: If the store verifies a Domain property in Search Console instead of a URL-prefix property, then reporting covers shop., checkout. and blog. subdomains and both http and https and www variants in 1 place, instead of missing traffic that lives on an uncovered variant.

signal.check: Search Console is set up as a URL-prefix property, or several separate properties exist for different subdomains and protocols.

risk.note: Adding a property does not remove existing ones.

prerequisites: DNS access at the domain registrar
steps: Add a Domain property in Search Console.
Copy the TXT record into DNS at the registrar.
If verification fails, retry the next day; DNS propagation can be slow.
If DNS access is truly impossible, fall back to a URL-prefix property for the exact live URL and note the limitation.

test.method: Confirm data appears for all known subdomains within 2 to 3 days of verification.

title: Refresh stale page code, not only visible copy
hypothesis: If page source is checked for stale years, old asset names and leftover app code, not just the visible copy, then pages read as current because a page can look updated on screen while its source still carries a 2022 timestamp or an uninstalled app's orphaned metafields.

signal.check: View-source on a page shows an old year, stale asset names, or metafields from an app that is no longer installed.

expected_effect.size: one audit spotted 2022 and 2023 timestamps still present in a page's source

prerequisites: View-source access
A list of uninstalled apps
steps: View source on key templates and search for outdated years and asset names.
Check product metafields for orphaned data from uninstalled review or app tools.
Remove stale code and metafields.
Update visible dates and years to match reality.

test.method: Recheck view-source after the cleanup for any remaining stale references.

title: Document technical gaps the team cannot yet solve instead of inventing a fix
hypothesis: If technical gaps the team lacks a proven answer for (hreflang and multi-region, deep pagination, crawl budget at scale, a full migration) are written down as open items instead of guessed at, then the store avoids acting on invented advice for a problem no source in the library actually covers.

signal.check: A technical question outside the covered rules (hreflang, deep pagination, crawl budget, migration) is being answered with a guess instead of a documented gap and a plan to research it.

prerequisites: None
steps: When a technical question falls outside the store's current SEO knowledge base, write it down as an open gap.
State what is unknown rather than guessing at a fix.
Research the specific current guidance before acting, especially for hreflang, pagination, crawl budget or a migration.
Track resolved gaps so the same question is not re-opened later.

test.method: Review the open-gaps list each quarter and confirm no guessed fix went live without research.

title: Treat mobile as the primary storefront design target, not a speed footnote
hypothesis: If navigation, filters, checkout and the product page are checked on a phone before a desktop screen, then the store fixes the experience most of its shoppers actually use, because most India-market and mobile-heavy US catalogs get the bulk of their sessions and revenue on mobile.
does_not_apply_when: The brand's own data shows most sessions and revenue come from desktop

signal.check: The store's own session and revenue split shows mobile as the majority, but design and QA reviews still check desktop first.

risk.note: Review process and design priority change only.

prerequisites: GA4 mobile share of sessions and revenue
steps: Pull GA4's mobile share of sessions and revenue to confirm mobile is the primary channel.
Check navigation, filters, checkout and product pages on a real phone before checking desktop.
Fix any mobile-specific issue (tap targets, filter usability, checkout friction) ahead of desktop polish.
Make mobile QA the default check for every new page or template.

test.method: Track mobile conversion rate and bounce rate before and after the mobile-first review process.
test.read_point: 8 to 12 weeks after adopting the process

title: Build region-specific pages for a store selling into more than 1 country or language
hypothesis: If a store selling into more than 1 region or language builds region-specific pages (currency, shipping terms, relevant local phrasing) with hreflang or a clear switcher, then shoppers in each region see the right offer because 1 generic page for both India and US traffic hides currency and shipping facts that differ by region.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells into only 1 country and language

signal.check: The store sells into more than 1 country or language but shows the same page with the same currency and shipping terms to all of them.

risk.note: hreflang misconfiguration can confuse search engines; test carefully before rolling out to all regions.

prerequisites: Confirmed regions and languages served
Currency and shipping terms per region
steps: List every region and language the store actually sells into.
Build or configure region-specific pages with the right currency and shipping terms.
Add hreflang tags or a clear, visible language and region switcher.
Avoid running 1 generic page across regions with materially different terms.

test.method: Compare conversion rate by region before and after region-specific pages go live.

title: Never buy or swap links; disclose any sponsored placement with rel=sponsored
hypothesis: If the store never buys or swaps links for discounts and marks any disclosed sponsored placement with rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow", then the link profile stays clean because paid and undisclosed links risk a manual action that can undo months of other SEO work.

signal.check: A link plan or vendor proposal includes paying for links, swapping links for a discount, or bulk link packages with no disclosure.

prerequisites: None
steps: Write the no-paid-links, no-swap policy into the link plan document.
Require any accepted sponsored placement to carry rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow" and be disclosed.
Decline any vendor or host that will not disclose a paid placement.
Review any past paid placement and fix the rel attribute if missing.

test.method: Audit the link log each month for undisclosed paid or swapped links.

title: Point earned links at educational pages and the root domain, then pass authority inward
hypothesis: If earned links target educational pages and the root domain first, then pass authority to money pages through internal links, the link profile looks natural because heavy direct linking to shopping pages reads as manipulative.

signal.check: Most or all earned links point directly to product or collection pages instead of educational content or the homepage.

expected_effect.size: one example allocates 50 to 75% of new links to the root domain in the first 3 months and 25 to 50% to collections ranking 4 to 10

prerequisites: Educational content or guides already published to receive links
steps: Prioritize link outreach toward guides, calculators and the homepage over product pages.
Pass authority inward from those pages to money pages using internal links.
Track the ratio of links landing on educational pages versus product pages.
Avoid ever building far more links to 1 product page than competitors have.

test.method: Review the link log each month for target-page mix.

title: Build local citations and NAP consistency only for stores with a physical location
hypothesis: If a store with a physical location keeps a consistent name, address and phone number across a small number of relevant directories, refreshed every 6 to 12 months, then local search visibility improves because inconsistent NAP data confuses local ranking signals.
does_not_apply_when: The store is a pure online retailer with no physical location or storefront

signal.check: The store has a physical location but its name, address or phone number differs across directory listings.

prerequisites: Confirmed physical location
The exact name, address and phone number to use everywhere
steps: List every directory currently carrying the store's listing.
Correct any mismatched name, address or phone number.
Keep the citation set small and relevant rather than mass-submitting to every directory.
Refresh the listings every 6 to 12 months.

test.method: Recheck directory listings for consistency at each refresh cycle.

title: Screen every link prospect with a fixed checklist before any outreach
hypothesis: If every prospect is screened for topic coherence, clean domain history, relevance, real traffic and a clean backlink profile before outreach, then link building effort avoids link farms and penalized sites because a real single-topic site with stable traffic is far more likely to produce a safe, useful link.

signal.check: Link prospects are contacted with no domain-history check, traffic check or relevance screen first.

risk.note: Screening step only, before any outreach is sent.

prerequisites: A backlink or authority tool
Access to the Wayback Machine
steps: Confirm the prospect is a real, coherent single-topic site, not a link farm.
Check its Wayback Machine history for a former unrelated use (a casino, a defunct business).
Confirm topical relevance to the store's category, direct or adjacent.
Check for at least about 1,000 monthly visits with no sudden traffic drop, and a clean backlink profile of its own.
Reject any Fiverr-style offer, unsolicited link seller or upfront payment request that is not a disclosed sponsored placement.
Record the target page on your own site and the reason the host would link.

test.method: Track what share of screened prospects convert to a real, safe link.

title: Sign up for journalist query platforms and answer relevant questions daily
hypothesis: If the store's named expert answers relevant journalist queries daily on a platform like Featured.com or Connectively, then it earns editorial links and mentions because journalist platforms convert first-hand expertise into real backlinks at low cost.

signal.check: No one at the brand is registered as a source on a journalist query platform, or queries are being answered with only a plain Google search instead of real expertise.

expected_effect.size: sources report roughly 1 hit per 100 submissions, or a 20-to-2-to-1 funnel

prerequisites: A named expert at the brand with a short bio
15 minutes a day available
steps: Sign up on a journalist query platform and claim the core niche and adjacent topics.
Filter by topic relevance, not by outlet size or deadline.
Research each answer from first-hand experience, not just a quick search; bold key phrases and use bullets.
Track query, outlet, pitch date and outcome in a sheet; reply to follow-ups before the deadline.

test.method: Track placements and links earned per month against submissions made.

title: Pitch guest posts and link inserts only with a real value offer, disclosed if paid
hypothesis: If guest post and link insert pitches always offer a real value (a tested, current replacement for an outdated page, or content the host's readers need) and any paid placement is disclosed with the correct rel attribute, then the store earns placements that pass Google policy instead of risking a penalty.

signal.check: Outreach emails use a generic template with no specific value offer, or a paid placement is being arranged without disclosure.

expected_effect.size: personalized pitches are estimated to beat about 70% of template-only outreach

risk.note: Decline any host that will not disclose a paid placement.

prerequisites: A screened prospect list (SEO-106)
steps: Personalize every pitch with a concrete, specific value offer for that host.
Write to the host's audience at 600 to 1,200 words unless told otherwise, with the link in a relevant sentence near the top using a soft anchor.
If the host asks for a fee, treat it as a disclosed sponsored placement with rel="sponsored" or decline.
After publishing, confirm the link is live, the rel attribute matches the deal, and the host did not alter the store's claims.

test.method: Track placement rate and rel-attribute compliance across a batch of pitches.

title: Run a backlink audit and disavow only with manual action or clear spam evidence
hypothesis: If a backlink audit checks Manual Actions and link-scheme history first and reserves disavow for manipulative links tied to an actual or likely manual action, then the store avoids removing links that were never actually hurting it, since most sites never need to disavow anything.

signal.check: A backlink audit is being planned or a disavow file is being built based on a spam-score band alone, with no Manual Actions check.

risk.note: A disavow file can be replaced, but an unnecessary disavow can remove links that were actually helping.

prerequisites: A backlink tool export
Search Console Manual Actions access
steps: Check Security and Manual Actions in Search Console first.
Sort referring domains by authority and spam score, but do not treat a low score alone as proof of harm.
Review the Lost and Vital view for high-authority links that disappeared and reach out about restoring them.
Disavow only manipulative links tied to an actual or likely manual action, uploading 1 domain or URL per line.

test.method: If a manual action exists, confirm it clears on re-review after disavowing.
test.read_point: after the next Search Console re-review

title: Do traditional SEO fundamentals first, before any AI answer-engine visibility work
hypothesis: If the store finishes its core Google and Bing SEO fundamentals before adding AI answer-engine work, then AI visibility improves faster because most AI answer engines retrieve from pages that already rank in traditional search.

signal.check: AI-visibility work (citation checks, llms.txt, prompt research) is starting before the store's core SEO fundamentals (technical floor, money pages) are done.

prerequisites: Technical floor and money pages already addressed
steps: Confirm the technical floor, money pages and first content cluster are in place.
Only then start dedicated AI-visibility checks and content formats.
Route deeper AI-search research (fan-out modelling, brand sentiment) to the AI-answer-engine playbook once fundamentals are solid.

test.method: Track AI citation appearances before and after fundamentals are confirmed solid.

title: Build the specific page formats AI answers actually cite: comparisons, buying guides, best-of roundups
hypothesis: If content investment favors product pages, comparisons, buying guides and best-of roundups with direct answers under clear headings, then AI-answer citations increase because these formats made up over half of citations in a large study of AI answers.

signal.check: The content plan has no comparison, buying-guide or best-of roundup pages for categories where AI answers already appear.

expected_effect.size: a cited study of over 768,000 AI citations found more than half came from product pages, comparisons and buying guides

prerequisites: A content cluster plan already in place (SEO-074)
steps: Identify categories where an AI answer already cites a competitor or a third party.
Prioritize comparisons, buying guides and best-of roundups for those categories.
Structure each with a direct answer near the top under a clear heading.
Pre-build assets for likely follow-up questions (alternatives, reviews, comparisons).

test.method: Check AI answers for the target queries monthly for citation of the store's pages.

title: Fix the Shopify global catalog and AI crawler access for AI shopping visibility
hypothesis: If the Shopify global product catalog is complete (title, image, non-zero price, terms compliance) and AI crawlers are deliberately allowed, then products can be found, matched and chosen by AI shopping tools because a stale or incomplete catalog and blocked crawlers hide the product from AI-driven discovery.

signal.check: The Shopify global catalog has products missing a title, image or price, or stale metafields, or AI crawlers are blocked without a deliberate decision.

prerequisites: Shopify admin access to catalog and crawler settings
steps: Check the global product catalog for title, at least 1 image, non-zero price and terms compliance on every product.
Clean up stale metafields left by uninstalled apps.
Confirm the store's AI crawler settings (agentic storefront and similar) reflect a deliberate decision, not a default.
Run the robots.txt curl check for named AI crawlers.

test.method: Recheck catalog completeness and crawler access monthly.

title: Measure AI visibility monthly with 3 labeled methods, not a crawler hit alone
hypothesis: If AI visibility is measured monthly through a manual incognito buying-question check, Search Console's generative AI report, and a paid tracker if available, each labeled by method, then the store gets an honest read because a crawler hit in server logs is not the same thing as a citation.

signal.check: AI visibility is reported as a single number with no note on which method produced it, or a crawler log hit is being counted as a citation.

expected_effect.size: one example scored 50 of 100 in the US market and was mentioned by Google AI Overviews but rarely by ChatGPT

prerequisites: Search Console's generative AI report (if available)
An incognito AI chat
steps: Ask 5 real buying-journey questions in an incognito AI chat and record which brands and pages are named.
Check Search Console's generative AI report if available.
Add a paid AI-visibility tracker only if the brand already pays for one.
Set the region to the brand's main market and label each number by its source method.
Never count a crawler hit in server logs as a citation.

test.method: Track the 3 labeled measures monthly and compare trend, not absolute score, across tools.

title: Never sell or rely on llms.txt as an AI-SEO fix
hypothesis: If llms.txt is never presented as equal to robots.txt or as a fix that improves AI visibility, then the store avoids a false promise because Google does not use it and other engines' support is unverified.

signal.check: A report, vendor pitch or internal plan claims llms.txt will improve AI visibility.

risk.note: Expectation-setting only; creating the file itself is harmless.

prerequisites: None
steps: If an llms.txt file is created, treat it as harmless housekeeping, not a ranking or citation fix.
Correct any claim that it is the AI equivalent of robots.txt.
Re-check adoption by AI engines periodically before revisiting this position.

test.method: Check whether any measurable AI citation change follows adding llms.txt, to confirm it has no independent effect.
test.read_point: next monthly AI visibility check after adding the file

title: Prioritize AI answer-engine visibility work for comparison-heavy and considered-purchase categories
hypothesis: If AI answer-engine visibility work is concentrated on comparison-heavy, considered or subscription categories rather than a single commodity SKU, then the AI-visibility effort pays off faster because these categories are the ones where AI answers most often surface comparisons and citations.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells 1 simple commodity SKU with little comparison shopping behavior

signal.check: AI-visibility work is spread evenly across the whole catalog instead of focused on comparison-heavy or considered-purchase categories.

prerequisites: Category list with purchase-consideration level noted
steps: Identify which categories are comparison-heavy, considered-purchase or subscription-based.
Prioritize AI-visibility content (SEO-111) and measurement (SEO-113) for those categories first.
Deprioritize AI-visibility work for single, low-consideration commodity SKUs.

test.method: Compare AI citation rate for prioritized categories versus deprioritized ones after 2 to 3 months.

title: Record a dated SEO baseline in the brand record before touching anything
hypothesis: If Search Console clicks, impressions, indexed counts, GA4 organic sessions and money-keyword positions are all recorded with a date before any SEO change starts, then later results can be proven because there is a real number to compare against.

signal.check: No dated SEO baseline exists in the brand record before starting or restarting work.

prerequisites: Search Console and GA4 already installed (P1)
steps: Record 3 months of Search Console clicks, impressions, CTR and average position, split branded vs non-branded.
Record indexed vs not-indexed page counts.
Record GA4 organic sessions and purchases by landing page.
Record current positions for the money-keyword shortlist and the referring-domain count.
Date the entry and store it in the brand record.

test.method: Compare every future report against this dated baseline.

title: Run a quick speed pass (images and apps) before escalating to a full speed project
hypothesis: If images and unused apps are fixed first as a quick pass, then most of the cheap speed gain is captured before deciding whether a full speed project is needed, because Core Web Vitals only becomes an SEO blocker when Poor URL groups show up on money templates.

signal.check: Search Console's Core Web Vitals report flags Poor groups on money templates, but no quick image or app fix has been tried yet.

prerequisites: PageSpeed Insights access
steps: Count Poor URL groups on mobile for product and collection templates in Search Console's Core Web Vitals report.
Compress, resize and lazy-load images (except the LCP image) sitewide.
Uninstall unused apps and remove their leftover theme code; load remaining app scripts only where needed.
Re-test; if Poor groups remain, hand the report to a full speed project.

test.method: Re-run PageSpeed Insights and recheck Poor group count 28 days after the fixes (field data lag).

title: Follow a fixed 30-day and 90-day sequence when starting or restarting SEO
hypothesis: If a new or restarted SEO program follows a fixed 30-day and 90-day sequence (tooling and keywords, then the top money page, then a cluster, then outreach), then the store sees real progress in the first quarter because the sequence forces money pages and technical fixes before any content or link work starts.

signal.check: SEO work is starting or restarting with no written 30-day or 90-day sequence.

prerequisites: P1 baseline recorded (SEO-116)
steps: Week 1: Search Console, tooling and 10 to 15 target keywords, with intent tests on the top 5.
Week 2: build or optimize the single most important money page.
Week 3: publish the first cluster piece linked to it.
Week 4: start journalist queries (15 minutes a day), an AI-visibility check, and the first Search Console read.
Months 2 to 3: finish 1 full content cluster and internal linking, then start link outreach and refreshes.
Day 90: re-benchmark rankings, non-branded clicks and organic revenue before choosing the next category.

test.method: Compare organic revenue and non-branded clicks at day 90 against the day-1 baseline.

title: Install GA4 and Search Console before launch and keep them separate
hypothesis: If GA4 and Search Console are both installed before launch and kept conceptually separate, then reporting stays reliable because GA4 has no backfill and Search Console shows how Google sees the site while GA4 shows what visitors do.

signal.check: GA4 or Search Console is missing, was installed late, or reports mix Search Console and GA4 numbers as if they measured the same thing.

prerequisites: Access to install tracking tags
steps: Install Search Console and GA4 before or as early as possible after launch.
Never install 2 GA4 tags on the same site.
Keep Search Console (how Google sees the site) and GA4 (what visitors do) as separate report sections.
Note that GA4 has no backfill, so any gap in early installation is a permanent data gap.

test.method: Confirm both tools show live data within 2 to 3 days of installation.

title: Report branded and non-branded clicks separately every month
hypothesis: If branded and non-branded clicks are always reported as separate lines, then the SEO program is judged fairly because branded volume often moves with ad spend, not SEO work, and mixing them hides whether non-branded search is actually growing.

signal.check: The monthly report shows only a combined total click number with no branded and non-branded split.

prerequisites: A regex filter for the brand's own names
steps: Filter queries with a regex that matches brand and product names for the branded line.
Filter the inverse ("doesn't match") for the non-branded line.
Compare the last 3 months to the previous period for each line separately.
Export the data before it ages out of Search Console's 16-month window.

test.method: Track non-branded clicks specifically as the leading SEO health indicator.

title: Read leading indicators before clicks in the first months of a new SEO program
hypothesis: If rising impressions, new untargeted queries and positions moving from page 5 toward page 3 are tracked in the first months, then early progress is visible before clicks catch up, because clicks lag behind these earlier signals.

signal.check: Early-stage SEO progress is judged only on clicks, with impressions and position movement ignored.

prerequisites: Search Console query and position data
steps: Track rising impressions and new, previously untargeted queries appearing.
Track positions moving from far pages (5+) toward page 3.
Ignore small wobbles (a 2-position shift on about 40 impressions) as noise.
Report these leading indicators alongside clicks in the first few months.

test.method: Check whether clicks eventually follow the leading indicators in the months after they first appear.

title: Push pages at positions 4 to 30 with impressions before writing anything new
hypothesis: If pages already ranking between positions 4 and 30 with real impressions are pushed with on-page work, internal links and a supporting piece, then the fastest wins are captured first because these pages are already close to page 1, unlike a brand-new page starting from nothing.

signal.check: The content queue has new pages ahead of any push work on existing pages ranking 4 to 30 with impressions.

risk.note: Prioritization and on-page work, previous copy saved.

prerequisites: Search Console query data filtered to positions 4 to 30
steps: Filter Search Console queries to positions 4 to 30 with real impressions.
Prioritize these pages ahead of any brand-new content this month.
Add on-page improvements, internal links from stronger pages, and a supporting piece if useful.
Recheck position and clicks after the push.

test.method: Compare position and clicks 4 to 8 weeks after pushing a low-hanging-fruit page.

title: Diagnose a high-impression, low-click page by position before touching the title
hypothesis: If a high-impression, low-click page is diagnosed by its position first, then the right fix gets applied because a page 2 or 3 problem needs content and links while a page 1 problem needs a title, meta or speed fix, and a stable position with falling CTR usually means a stale snippet or an AI Overview now sits above it.

signal.check: A page shows high impressions and low clicks, and the fix applied does not match its actual position (for example, rewriting a title on a page 2 result).

expected_effect.size: 1 example showed 74,000 impressions to 175 clicks and another 46,000 to 6

risk.note: Diagnostic step, fix applied is independently reversible.

prerequisites: Search Console position data for the affected query
steps: Check the average position for the high-impression, low-click query.
If page 2 or 3: work content and internal links, not the title.
If page 1: rewrite the title and meta, compare against competing snippets, and check speed.
If position is stable but CTR is falling, check for a new AI Overview above the result and go deeper than it.

test.method: Re-measure CTR on the same query set 4 weeks after the matching fix.

title: Diagnose a traffic drop by finding what the losing pages share
hypothesis: If a traffic drop is diagnosed by sorting a 6-month comparison by click difference and looking for a shared trait among the losers (1 cluster, 1 template, thin copy, cannibalization, a changed SERP), then the real cause gets fixed instead of guessed at.

signal.check: Organic clicks or revenue have dropped and no one has sorted pages by click difference to find the shared cause.

prerequisites: 6-month Search Console comparison data
steps: Set the comparison window to cover the drop (6 months vs previous).
Sort pages by click difference ascending to find the biggest losers.
Look for a shared trait: 1 cluster, 1 template, thin copy, 2 pages competing on 1 keyword, a lost redirect, a new noindex.
Check the date against known theme changes, app installs, migrations or a Google update.
Fix the largest losers first and log the fix.

test.method: Check whether clicks on the fixed pages recover in the next 2 monthly reads.
test.read_point: next 2 monthly reads after the fix

title: Retarget a page's title and H1 to the query that actually earns its clicks
hypothesis: If a page's title and H1 are retargeted to whichever query is actually earning it clicks, not the originally intended keyword, then clicks increase because the page may already be answering a slightly different question than it was built for.

signal.check: A page's Queries tab in Search Console shows a different top click-earning query than its current title and H1 target.

expected_effect.size: one example moved from 3 clicks in 3 months on the original phrasing to 19 clicks on the actual click-earning phrasing

prerequisites: Search Console Queries tab filtered by page
steps: Filter Search Console by the page and open its Queries tab.
Compare the intended target keyword against the actual click leader.
If they differ, retarget the title and H1 to the click-leading query.
Recheck clicks after the change.

test.method: Compare clicks on the query before and after retargeting.

title: Track organic add-to-cart, checkout and purchase by landing page, not just clicks
hypothesis: If organic add-to-cart, begin-checkout and purchase events are tracked by landing page, then a mid-funnel collapse gets investigated before anyone touches keywords, because a page can gain clicks and still lose revenue if the funnel breaks after the click.

signal.check: GA4 tracks organic sessions but not add-to-cart, checkout and purchase events broken out by landing page.

prerequisites: GA4 ecommerce events configured
Tag Manager if button-click tracking is needed
steps: Confirm add-to-cart, begin-checkout and purchase events fire correctly for organic sessions.
Break these out by landing page in GA4 reporting.
When clicks rise but revenue does not, check the funnel step by step before touching keywords.
Never read 1 metric alone; check the whole funnel together.

test.method: Investigate any page where clicks grew but purchases did not, before making a keyword change.

title: Set a fixed cadence for keyword tracking, GSC and GA4 review, and device or country splits
hypothesis: If 20 to 30 money keywords are tracked weekly, Search Console and GA4 are reviewed monthly, and device and country splits are reviewed quarterly, then nothing important gets missed because each cadence matches how fast that data actually moves.

signal.check: There is no fixed schedule for keyword tracking, monthly reviews or device and country splits.

prerequisites: A rank tracking tool for 20 to 30 keywords
steps: Track 20 to 30 money keywords weekly.
Review Search Console and GA4 together monthly.
Review device and country splits quarterly.
Put these 3 cadences on the shared team calendar.

test.method: Confirm each cadence is actually run on schedule for 1 full quarter.

title: Lead every monthly SEO report with organic revenue, not vanity totals
hypothesis: If the monthly report leads with organic revenue and non-branded clicks, then money-keyword positions, indexed pages, links earned and AI mentions, then the reader sees what matters first because vanity totals like raw traffic or blog output do not show whether the program is paying back.

signal.check: The current monthly report template leads with sessions, page count or blog output instead of organic revenue.

prerequisites: Organic revenue tracked by GA4
steps: Put organic revenue and organic purchases as the first section of the report.
Follow with non-branded clicks, money-keyword positions and indexed money pages.
Add links earned, refreshes published and AI-visibility notes after that.
Remove or demote any vanity total (raw sessions, blog post count) from the top of the report.

test.method: Confirm every future report follows this order.

title: Do not build a custom dashboard until a free template or export stops being enough
hypothesis: If reporting runs on a free template or a direct export until that genuinely stops being enough, then time is not spent building and maintaining a custom dashboard the store does not yet need.

signal.check: A custom dashboard project is being proposed before a simple export or free template has been tried and found insufficient.

prerequisites: None
steps: Try a free reporting template or a direct export first.
Note specifically what it cannot do before proposing a custom dashboard.
Only build a custom dashboard once the free option demonstrably fails a real need.

test.method: Track how long the free template or export serves the reporting need before it is replaced.
test.read_point: each time reporting needs are reviewed

title: Triage bounce rate on content pages, excluding checkout and confirmation pages
hypothesis: If bounce rate triage excludes checkout, confirmation and gift-card pages and focuses on content pages over about 50%, then real thin or old copy gets found because those excluded page types are supposed to have high bounce and are not a real signal of a content problem.

signal.check: A bounce rate review includes checkout, confirmation or gift-card pages in the same list as content pages.

prerequisites: GA4 bounce rate by page
steps: Exclude checkout, confirmation and gift-card pages from the bounce review.
List content pages with bounce rate over about 50%.
Check each for thin or old copy and refresh candidates (SEO-079).
Recheck bounce rate after the refresh.

test.method: Compare bounce rate on flagged pages before and after a refresh.

title: Run the full technical SEO audit checklist quarterly, working errors first
hypothesis: If the full technical audit checklist (indexing, duplication, robots, sitemap, canonicals, headings, structured data, orphans, image weight, Core Web Vitals) is run every quarter as a single pass, then technical drift is caught before it costs real traffic instead of being found by accident.

signal.check: No quarterly technical audit has been run against the full checklist in the last 3 months.

risk.note: Audit pass; each fix is independently reversible.

prerequisites: A crawler and Search Console access
steps: Run the full checklist: indexing, URL duplication, tag pages, robots.txt, sitemap, 404s, canonicals, headings, titles and metas, structured data, JS-only content, orphans, image weight, Core Web Vitals, leftover app code, video pages, code freshness.
Work every error found before any warning or notice.
Log each fix with the date.
Schedule the next run for the following quarter.

test.method: Compare error count quarter over quarter.

title: Audit every competing collection page against the full collection template checklist
lever: collection page audit as recurring action
hypothesis: If every collection page competing for a real term is checked against the full template checklist (title, H1, description length, grid, FAQ, reviews, schema, images, internal links), then weak collection pages get found and fixed on a schedule instead of only when a problem is noticed.

signal.check: No structured audit of collection pages against the full template checklist has been run recently.

risk.note: Audit pass; each fix independently reversible.

prerequisites: List of competing collection pages
steps: For each collection page, check for cannibalization, page-type match, title, H1, URL, short and detailed description, grid settings, subcollections, facets, FAQ, reviews, meta, schema, images and internal links.
Log every gap found against the checklist.
Prioritize fixes on the highest-traffic collections first.
Re-audit on a fixed schedule (quarterly or after a major catalog change).

test.method: Track how many checklist gaps close each cycle and the resulting change in clicks.

title: Audit every optimized product page against the full product template checklist
lever: product page audit as recurring action
hypothesis: If every optimized product page is checked against the full template checklist (index decision, title, copy stack, facts, images, reviews, schema, rendering, variants, breadcrumbs), then weak product pages are caught on a schedule instead of drifting unnoticed.

signal.check: No structured audit of product pages against the full template checklist has been run recently.

risk.note: Audit pass; each fix independently reversible.

prerequisites: List of optimized product pages
steps: For each product page, check the index decision, title and H1, copy stack, explicit facts, images, reviews and schema, JavaScript-off rendering, variants, breadcrumbs, meta description, URL handle and out-of-stock handling.
Log every gap found against the checklist.
Prioritize fixes on the highest-traffic products first.
Re-audit on a fixed schedule.

test.method: Track checklist gap closure and the resulting change in clicks and conversion.

title: Review the keyword map against its own checklist before trusting it
hypothesis: If the keyword map is reviewed against a fixed checklist (stated floor, difficulty ceiling, intent per row, SERP check done, no duplicate primaries, clusters, gaps mapped, status and owner), then the map stays trustworthy because a map built once and never re-checked drifts out of date.

signal.check: The keyword map has not been reviewed against its own quality checklist since it was first built.

prerequisites: An existing keyword map (SEO-027)
steps: Confirm the volume floor and difficulty ceiling are still stated and current.
Confirm every row has an intent label matching its page type.
Confirm every row has a dated SERP check and no 2 rows share a primary keyword.
Confirm gaps, status and owner columns are filled in and shortlist items are prioritized over volume-sorted long tail.
Fix any gap found.

test.method: Recheck the map against the checklist each quarter.

title: Run the monthly Search Console read as a fixed checklist, not an ad-hoc glance
lever: monthly SC read as recurring action
hypothesis: If the monthly Search Console read always covers the same fixed checklist (branded vs non-branded, impressions trend, biggest losers, CTR triage, low-hanging fruit, unanswered questions, not-indexed money pages, Core Web Vitals, schema errors, new referring sites, AI impressions), then nothing gets missed month to month because the read does not depend on memory.

signal.check: The monthly Search Console review is done ad hoc with no fixed checklist, and some months skip sections like schema errors or new referring sites.

prerequisites: Domain property with 3 or more months of data
steps: Pull Performance data for the last 3 months vs the previous period, split branded and non-branded.
Sort Pages by click difference to find losers, and by impressions with low clicks for CTR triage.
Pull positions 4 to 30 with impressions and new untargeted queries.
Check the question regex for unanswered queries and the Indexing, Core Web Vitals, Shopping and Enhancements reports.
Check Links for top pages and new referring sites, and the generative AI report if available.
Export the data and save it dated for the record.

test.method: Confirm every checklist section was completed each month for a full quarter.

title: Run a periodic content refresh review across the whole site, not just 1 page at a time
lever: content refresh review as recurring action
hypothesis: If a periodic review checks every candidate page (positions 4 to 30, falling CTR, click losers, year-stamped titles) against a fixed checklist (click leader match, SERP format, depth, human moat, citations, internal links, dates, voice, cannibalization), then refresh work happens on a schedule instead of only when someone happens to notice a stale page.

signal.check: No periodic sitewide content refresh review has been run; refreshes only happen when someone notices a problem by chance.

risk.note: Review pass; each refresh independently reversible with saved copy.

prerequisites: Content inventory with URL, keyword and status
steps: Build the candidate list: positions 4 to 30 with impressions, falling CTR at a stable position, click losers, and year-stamped titles.
For each candidate, check the click-leader match, whether the SERP format changed, depth versus the top 5, human-moat presence, citations, internal links, dates and voice.
Fix cannibalization if 1 query switches between URLs.
Log every refresh with the date and re-read results 4 to 8 weeks later.

test.method: Compare clicks, impressions and position for refreshed pages against the pre-refresh window.

title: Screen every SEO pitch for red flags before hiring an agency, freelancer or tool
hypothesis: If every SEO pitch is screened for red flags (a guaranteed rank, a bloated audit, cheap bulk links, blog-only retainers, tool advice from someone paid by the tool), then the store avoids paying for vanity work because knowing a tool is not the same as knowing SEO, and no vendor can actually promise a rank.

signal.check: A new SEO pitch, audit or retainer is being considered without checking it against a fixed red-flag list.

expected_effect.size: one named example was about $400 a month for 3 blog posts only, with no site structure work

risk.note: Screening step only, before any contract is signed.

prerequisites: The vendor's pitch, audit sample or retainer proposal
steps: Check for a guaranteed rank, cheap bulk links, or "our content ranks number 1" language.
Check whether the audit lists dozens of critical fixes beyond the 4 technical essentials, a sign of a sales document.
Check whether the retainer only covers blog posts and never touches collection or product page structure.
Ask whether the vendor is paid by any tool they recommend.

test.method: Track how many red flags a pitch trips before deciding to hire.

title: Ask for a named past client site and dates before hiring any link or SEO vendor
hypothesis: If a vendor is asked for 1 named past client site with campaign start and end dates, and that site's traffic trend is checked across the window, then a vendor whose past work actually caused a decline gets refused before any money changes hands.

signal.check: A vendor is being considered without providing a named client site with specific campaign dates to verify.

expected_effect.size: one example showed a highly rated freelancer's own client site with a declining traffic line across the claimed window

prerequisites: A traffic estimation tool to check the named site
steps: Ask the vendor for 1 named past client site and the exact campaign start and end dates.
Check that site's traffic trend across the stated window in a keyword or traffic tool.
Treat a declining trend during the claimed campaign as a refusal.
Refuse any vendor who will not name a real client site.

test.method: Track hire decisions made with versus without this check over time.

title: Set a 3-to-6-month organic revenue review window with the baseline recorded first
hypothesis: If any SEO engagement (in-house or agency) is judged on organic revenue after 3 to 6 months, with the store's own before-data recorded at the start, then the decision to continue or stop is based on real payback instead of a gut feeling or vanity metrics.

signal.check: An SEO engagement has no stated review window or no recorded before-data to compare against.

prerequisites: The SEO baseline (SEO-116)
steps: Record organic revenue, non-branded clicks and money-keyword positions before the engagement starts.
Set a fixed 3-to-6-month review date in the agreement or plan.
At the review date, compare organic revenue against the baseline, not against blog output or ranking counts alone.
Decide continue, adjust or stop based on that comparison.

test.method: Compare organic revenue at the review date against the recorded baseline.
test.read_point: 3 to 6 months after the engagement starts
